speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgency. speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: TORONTO INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT AND MONTREAL DORVAL AIRPORT
speechtext:
1. Since the opening of Terminal 2 at Toronto International Airport, the average number of flights per week at Terminal 1 have been 1,124 and 1,539 at Terminal 2. In the corresponding period the average number of flights per week at Dorval have been 2,347. There are 24 gates at Terminal 1 and 16 gates at Terminal 2; these are supplemented by off-gate aircraft positions to an extent which ordinarily raises the number of actual gate positions to 32 at Terminal 1 and 22 at Terminal 2. subsubtopic: CANADA-USSR FISHERIES AGREEMENT
speechtext: Has the government or government officials signed an agreement with the USSR that would allow the use of Tasu Inlet as an operational base for Soviet vessels and, if so, what was the basis for the said agreement and what are the particulars relating to the scope of the operation of Soviet vessels in this Inlet?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CANADA-USSR FISHERIES AGREEMENT
speechtext:
On January 22, 1971, an agreement was concluded with the USSR on co-operation in fisheries in the northeastern Pacific Ocean off the coast of Canada. The agreement came into force on February 19, 1971, for a two year period and was extended with amendments in February 1973 for a further two year period. Article VII of the agreement states; "The Government of Canada will permit fishing vessels of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics and their service vessels to conduct loading and unloading operations in Tasu Sound and in the territorial sea of Canada off the west coast of Moresby Island between 52 degrees 23 minutes north latitude and 52 degrees 56 minutes north latitude. Such vessels will be permitted to enter Tasu Sound through an entrance corridor of Canadian internal waters extending two miles to the south and two miles to the north of the centre line of the entrance to Tasu Sound. To ensure safe navigation each fishing or service vessel of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics must notify the Canadian Director of Fisheries, Pacific Region, through the radio stations at Victoria, Tofino or Bull Harbour, preferably twelve hours but in no case less than two hours in advance of its expected time of arrival at the entrance to Tasu Sound." The basis for this agreement is described in its preamble, which may be summarized as recognizing the mutual interest of both countries in co-operating on fisheries in the area, and in conducting operations on a scientific basis with due regard to conser-

November 19, 1973

vation. In particular, through this agreement the government of Canada secured the removal of Soviet trawlers from the Big Bank area on the high seas off the coast of Vancouver Island where there had been conflicts with the operations of Canadian fisherman. The agreement has operated to the satisfaction of both countries, as evidenced by its recent renewal.

However, as under an amendment made to the act in 1970, copies of the lists applicable to each electoral district were forwarded by the Chief Electoral Officer to the appropriate returning officer who had to make them available for inspection during the period of the general election by the candidates officially nominated in that electoral district, pursuant to subsection 28(1) of the act, a number of returning officers, including the returning officer for Gander-Twillingate, did add up the number of names on their lists and included the figure so obtained in their Recapitulation Sheets which served as the basis for the preparation of the statistical report published pursuant to subsection 58(9) of the act. It is hon. members who elect the Speaker, and there has to be some semblance of order in any kind of public assembly. Members in any assembly get together and choose one of their members, who is elected in the same way as all of them and who represents a number of constituents. That person is selected by the House, by his colleagues and peers, to try to have the rules respected. The Chair does not make the rules.
The hon. member suggests that the rules should be changed. I see nothing wrong with an evolving, moving and progressing institution such as parliament, and it may well be that the rule to which the hon. member takes exception is wrong and should be changed. But as long as it is there I am sure the hon. member himself would expect the Chair to see that this rule is enforced. It relates only to the use of certain words and certain language which when used, I suggest, complicates the proper conduct of our business. This is why I am asking the hon. member to change the wording that he has used. This is not the end of

the world. The hon. member has indicated that another member has misled the House, has given wrong information to the House. It is quite possible, according to the rules, to make that kind of charge. It is possible for a member to say of another member that he has given false information to the House, that he is wrong, that he is incorrect, indeed, that he is misleading the House. What is wrong is to charge another hon. member with deliberately misleading the House. This is a moral accusation, and I think that is why it is wrong. I doubt whether this is really what the hon. member wanted to do, and I hope he will find some way of assisting me in this respect.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at ten o'clock on last Thursday night we were discussing the merits of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). I heartily support the amendment for the reasons I detailed at that time.
I should like to point out that, with development and investment which affects the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, it is very important that the residents of the area have a say in what is to be allowed. Natural resources are vested in the provinces and under their provincial control; in the territories, they are under the control of the federal government so that decisions affecting the resources could be made without the people of the territories knowing anything about them. This is a very important matter in the Yukon and that portion of the Northwest Territories that is close to Alaska, because of the development following the discoveries made at Prudhoe Bay.
November 19, 1973

The Yukon and the Northwest Territories will be affected in years to come by what happens to the oil and gas in Alaska and the Mackenzie delta; presumably it will eventually come south. It has already been decided that an oil pipeline will run from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez, in spite of the discussion about the possibility of a Mackenzie valley pipeline. Should the pipeline through the Mackenzie valley come to pass, the question of Indian rights will be an important consideration. There has already been one very important court decision about the ownership of land in similar circumstances, the ecological effects of development and so on. It is important that the native people in the affected area have an input in all decisions. The United States has already decided upon the Alaskan oil pipeline. Had the alternative of the Mackenzie valley pipeline been decided upon, it would have meant a great deal of drilling and development work as much of the oil lies close to where the pipeline would go.
El Paso Natural Gas hopes to take gas from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez through a pipeline paralleling the Alaskan oil pipeline. In the Yukon and the Northwest Territories there are proven reserves of approximately seven trillion cubic feet, and it is estimated that there is another 100 trillion cubic feet in the Mackenzie valley and the Beaufort sea, while the North Slope has proven gas reserves of 26 trillion cubic feet and estimated reserves of up to 400 trillion cubic feet. This is more than double the potential reserves of the lower 48 states.
Similarly in the Canadian north, our proven and estimated reserves are double the reserves present in the northern frontier areas. Reserves of 7 trillion cubic feet are not enough to support a pipeline down the Mackenzie Valley to Canadian markets, and North Slope gas will be necessary if that pipeline is to be feasible. So it is most important, Mr. Speaker, that the people who live in those areas and who are represented by the territorial councils, should have some say about the possibility of a pipeline. If this is to come about we can estimate the cost at $5 billion. Most of this money will have to come from the great financial institutions to the south, and of course this investment will be reviewed by a board of civil servants based in Ottawa. It is easy to see, Mr. Speaker, that the decisions made could be detrimental to the people in the areas affected and to the development of those areas. I think it is important for those areas to which I have referred to be allowed to decide whether or not there is to be investment in those areas. Certainly, in northern Canada more than in southern Canada, it is likely that foreign investment will be necessary, as in the southern part of the country resources can be more easily developed without foreign participation.
It seems likely that El Paso will be required to move North Slope gas through Alaska. That is perhaps another reason why supporters of the Mackenzie Valley pipeline are not likely to see a pipeline built in the immediate future. It is a fact that many Canadians do not see the advantage of combining North Slope and Delta gas in one system. I say this because many feel that Canadian Delta gas should be left in the ground for some time into the future. I think this position is quite unrealistic. I think the development of the remote delta areas would bring impor-
Foreign Investment Review Act tant effects for those who live in the Yukon as well as in the Mackenzie Valley. Such development would lead to increased economic activity, that is, to greater development, more jobs and so on. Unless something like this is done, the development of these other areas may be seriously compromised.
To repeat, I support this amendment. I think it is necessary. I think amendments which give the provinces greater input in the decision-making process ought to be pushed strongly. The same argument applies even more strongly to the territories. They are a long way from Ottawa. The federal government owns the resources in the ground where the development will take place. I hope the government will see fit to accept the amendment at the proper time.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say a few words about the subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) to Motion No. 2, which stands in my name on behalf of my party. I say at the outset, as others have indicated, that the subamendment has merit. I support it wholeheartedly.
As I said earlier when I directed a question to the hon. member proposing the subamendment, it would be useful to have on record the definition of territory and territorial council, as those terms apply to this legislation. The relevant definition is set out in section 3.(1) of the Interpretation Act, which reads;
Every provision of this Act extends and applies, unless a contrary intention appears, to every enactment, whether enacted before or after the commencement of this Act.
The definition section of the Interpretation Act says:
'province' means a province of Canada, and includes the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories;
Having said that, I feel that I was perhaps derelict in not talking over that interpretation in the first place with the hon. member for Timiskaming when he introduced his subamendment.
As the hon. member who has just spoken said clearly, the territories need as much protection, as the provinces, if not more. The mineral wealth in provinces is under provincial jurisdiction, whereas the mineral wealth in the territories at present is under the jurisdiction and control of the federal government. The people in the Yukon and Northwest Territories do not have the protection of provincial legislatures. Their governing counsels do not have the vested interest in their resources which provinces have in theirs.
Basically, the hon. member for Timiskaming seems to be showing concern for the rights of the territories vis-a-vis the provinces. He is concerned about the status of the territories as compared with the status of the provinces, in much the same way as we are concerned about the status of the provinces, as compared with the powers and prerogatives of the federal government. It is wrong to suggest, as the minister has by implication, that in this amendment we are discussing the veto power of the provinces, a veto power over decisions made by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie). I do not think the minister meant to convey that impression so forcefully; certainly, it is not in accordance with the facts.

November 19, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
No one will argue that the bill, as drawn at present, gives the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce the ultimate power in deciding whether any foreign investment is of significant benefit for this nation. That is as it should be. Many members are concerned about the minister's curious reluctance to take into account the concerns of the provinces in this area and their very real desire to contribute to the various factors which the minister must consider in arriving at a decision. This is rather strange.
I do not wish to digress from the amendment or the general subject matter of the debate, but it is interesting to note that this government has adopted a somewhat inflexible attitude to what I consider to be a reasonable proposition, which is this. Before the government decides anything about the control of foreign investment, the provinces must be given maximum opportunities for consultation. Let me illustrate.
The United Kingdom, generally regarded as a more centralized state than ours, geographically and otherwise, with longer traditions in considering movements encouraging home rule for its various regions, implicit therein, has been considering some questions. For example, there is a major move to give greater powers to the various regions of the United Kingdom. I refer hon. members of the House to the royal commission studying these questions headed by Lord Kilbrandon. That commission rejected the case for granting complete sovereignty to an independent Scotland and Wales, on grounds that the majority simply did not want it. The U.K. Government is actively studying the problem. It is apparent that there is a move afoot in the United Kingdom to recognize some of the ancient prerogatives as well as current ambitions of territories and regions such as Scotland, Wales and England itself, which all are encompassed by the United Kingdom.
Let me read briefly from a recent news report carried in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald:
The report said dissatisfaction in Scotland is largely based on economic considerations. In Wales discontent is linked with a desire to preserve the Welsh language and culture.
Eleven members signed the report. The other two members produced a minority report calling for a wider interpretation of the commission's term of reference.
Of the 11 who signed the report, a majority favored a plan of devolution which would transfer to directly-elected Scottish and Welsh assemblies powers over local government, town and country planning, education and other services.
That shows that the United Kingdom is prepared to make greater concessions to certain regions than it has heretofore. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce ought to consider that fact on continuing condition terms.
It is obvious that the representations we made to the minister in committee have been considered. However, I do not think we persuaded him to be more flexible in allowing the provinces more input into his decisions. It is clear that the minister is continuing to be completely inflexible in this regard.
We welcome this subamendment moved by the hon. member for Timiskaming. He wishes to include the Northwest Territories and the Yukon in any consultative input which might be granted to the provinces. That the hon. member wishes to extend to the territories this kind of

right indicates that he and his colleagues of the NDP realize that the members of my party are not trying to hamstring the minister or the government in the advancement of legitimate Canadian nationalism. We are simply trying to give those parts of the country which are poorest by virtue of their economic circumstances as much influence as other parts of Canada might have. We want to give the people of those areas a meaningful opportunity to influence the minister.
In the absence of meaningful guidelines to foreign industry, I again plead with the minister to reconsider his attitude and to take note of the fact that apparently some members of the New Democratic Party are changing their minds about the effects of these amendments. They realize these amendments are not necessarily going to impede the efficient administration of this particular bill. Rather, they will simply make it a bit more open in so far as the provinces are concerned, and a bit more courtesy will be shown them with regard to what is happening. The provinces will be provided with information which I am sure they will regard as confidential, and in no way will the basic efforts the minister is attempting to make be impeded.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate on Bill C-132, I wish to make my position quite clear at the outset. While I am prepared to accept some of the amendments, I am not prepared to accept the bill as it now stands. I consider it to be totally unrealistic and unacceptable to the disadvantaged areas of this country. For that reason, I am not prepared to give it my support.
I have taken that position because I have a very good idea of the importance of foreign capital to certain regions of Canada. In particular, it is important to the province I know best, Newfoundland. I wish to make it perfectly clear also that we do not enjoy being dependent on foreign countries for our investment capital, but what choice have we had since becoming a province of this country in 1949?
Prior to confederation, there were three opposing forces in Newfoundland. One group supported the retention of the commission form of government that was imposed upon us by the British government in 1933. Another group supported a return of responsible government as it existed prior to 1933. The third group supported our becoming a province of Canada. A fourth group emerged some time later and advocated that we enter into economic union with the United States. I shall have more to say about that group later. The outcome of the ensuing referendum that was to decide our future is obvious because we are now the tenth province of Canada. There is very little to be gained or any justification for deliberating on past events or speculating on what could have been. However, there is a lesson to be learned from our past experiences as a province of Canada, and from re-assessing some of the shortcomings of confederation as they relate to our newest province.
In a great many respects, confederation has been very good for our people but, unfortunately, in certain respects it has been a dismal failure. I am afraid the bill we are now debating will add to our problems and further accen-
November 19, 1973

tuate the shortcomings of confederation as far as Newfoundland is concerned. For almost 25 years, we have been victims of the upper Canadian attitudes as expressed in their unwillingness to invest their capital outside of the golden triangle, or as my colleague, the member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) put it, their unwillingness to invest off the 401 highway.
This attitude on the part of the upper Canadian investors is reflected in this and previous governments with perhaps one exception, that is the administration of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). His heart was in the right place. He recognized the problems of the so-called have-not regions of this country. What is more important, he was prepared to do something about it, and would have, had he not trod on the corns of central Canada and posed a threat to their comfortable monopolistic position.
For an example, let us examine the 1973-74 estimates of the Department of Public Works. The total expenditure by that department in the Atlantic area under all headings is $27,776,000. In Newfoundland, it is $7,749,000. The proposed expenditure by the same department for the same period in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec is close to $300 million. This government is spending more money on cafeteria facilities, parking garages and air conditioning improvements in these two provinces than on harbour and wharf facilities in Newfoundland. One has to remember that the economy of Newfoundland depends to a large extent on the fisheries which, of course, depends on the provision of adequate fishing facilities such as breakwaters, wharves and good harbour facilities, all of which are the responsibility of the federal government. While I am not opposed to proper air conditioning, parking or cafeteria facilities for our public servants, I am opposed to their receiving priority consideration when they are secondary needs. I will, however, leave it to Your Honour's personal conclusion as to their relative importance to the well being of this country.
As a further illustration of this attitude, let us take a look at Canadian National, or perhaps I should say the Department of Transport because CN is a creature of the federal government and is answerable to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). Their misplaced policies are probably the biggest single threat to confederation. While they moan and groan about incurring deficits in maintaining essential services such as rail passenger services in the poorer provinces, they are willing to spend $21 million on a useless tower in Toronto which will provide a variety of services, including a bigger and more sophisticated communications system in an area where there is already accessibility to 10 or 11 TV channels. At the same time, there are thousands of people living in the remote parts of this country, including Newfoundland, where TV, telephone or indeed any means of communication continues to be another unfulfilled dream. Is it any wonder that we view with mistrust and suspicion any attempt on the part of this government to take complete control of our destinies.
Earlier in my speech I referred to the political situation in Newfoundland just prior to confederation. I mentioned the various groups that were vying for power, including a group of people, many of whom have since distinguished
Foreign Investment Review Act themselves in business and Canadian politics. These people advocated that Newfoundland enter into a form of economic union with the United States.
On March 28, 1948, they launched their party and their leader gave a very stirring speech on the Newfoundland radio stations. Let me read into the record, a portion of the speech made in Newfoundland on that date:
The goal of full employment for Newfoundlanders thus ensuring permanent prosperity for Newfoundland can only be obtained through economic union with the United States. There is no other course that can solve Newfoundland's problems. . ..
In the event of economic union with the United States millions of dollars of American capital will flow into this country to develop our natural resources. Look to our great possession Labrador. Look to its vast timber and mineral wealth. Think what it would mean to this country to have this priceless territory developed. American money can do that, American capital must do that if we are to have a better way of life.
I have put those words on record for a very good and obvious reason. The hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson) was obviously having a great deal of fun when he spoke on this bill last week. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) whom he followed in the debate, was, he said, singing "O Canada" to the tune of "God Bless America". In the years preceding Newfoundland's entry into confederation, the hon. minister was so busy extolling the virtues of Uncle Sam and the generosity of U.S. capital that he didn't have time even to learn the tune of "O Canada". The hon. member has proven beyond a doubt his ability to run with the hare and hunt with the hounds, because the words I have just quoted were written by him in 1948 in his role as chief propagandist and co-leader of the movement to have Newfoundland enter into an economic union with the United States. I am sure he has many memories, some of which must be embarrassing, of his involvement in that movement and the slogan he himself coined as its battle cry- "For a brighter tomorrow, vote economic union with the U.S. today".

speechtext:
Let us, for a moment, consider how other undeveloped areas thrive as compared to those closer to home. Though I do not wish to downgrade Canada's investment in other countries, I cannot help but think it is ironic that Canada continues to invest hundreds of millions of dollars in underdeveloped countries and, at the same time, justifies withholding assistance from the financially insecure provinces in its own country. International development is an infinitely complex field; it compounds the subtleties of social development and international relations with the difficulties of cross-cultural communication but its potential for good is incalculable. For example, corporations such as CIDA continue to grow steadily. Total funds made available by parliament in 1971-72 rose to $431 million an increase of almost $48 million compared with the preceding year.
Canadian business is a vital partner in the economic and social progress of developing countries. Under CIDA administration services and expertise may be found in more than 80 countries. Grants and long-term loans provided through CIDA offer a source of financing for Canadian goods and services. By helping low-income

November 19, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act countries achieve self-sustaining development, the Corporation assists in the expansion of world trade and increases the prospects for continuing exports of competitive Canadian products. I hate to say it, Mr. Speaker, but sometimes I wish Newfoundland were not part of Canada but, rather, a foreign country. Then, perhaps, we might at long last receive some type of assistance from this government.
From what I have said, Mr. Speaker, it is quite evident that Newfoundland should not have to go begging to foreign countries when we have such a prosperous country closer to home. But it seems that Newfoundland has no other choice than to do just that-to go abroad for assistance. Until I am convinced that the attitude of Canadian investors is changing or that the federal government is willing to pay more than mere lip service to the issue of regional disparity, I am not prepared to support any attempt on the part of the government or the financiers of Upper Canada to cut off our only real source of investment capital.
A lot of mistakes have been made in Newfoundland in recent years, but I contend that these mistakes and the losses arising therefrom are a direct result of the unwillingness of the Canadian government and private investors to recognize our need for assistance in developing our resources and diversifying our economy. As a province we have never pursued a policy of attracting foreign capital per se. Rather, our objective has always been simply to attract to the province sufficient development capital to enable us to attain our economic goals. As Canadians, we would prefer that this development capital be Canadian. Indeed, it has been most disenchanting to find, as Canada's newest province, that sufficient development funds have not been forthcoming from within our own country. Accordingly, as long as this situation continues, we have no choice but to welcome foreign investment under whatever terms and conditions are available. To demonstrate that sufficient development capital has not been forthcoming from Canada, one has only to examine the financing of recent major development projects in Newfoundland.
By now, everyone has heard of the Come-By-Chance oil refinery. The total investment of that refinery was in the area of $160 million, of which the government of Newfoundland contributed $30 million, and foreign investment $130 million. Nowhere do we see Canada putting up any money. Again, the second oil refinery proposed at Come-By-Chance will cost $308 million of which $78,500,000 will come from Newfoundland and $230 million from foreign investment. Again, we see no contribution, loan or grant made by Canada. A third example is the liner board mill in Stephenville. The total investment in this operation came to $160 million, of which $89 million came from outside this country. The province invested $73 million. Consider, in the light of these and similar figures, the role which foreign investment has played in the economic development of our province. One can appreciate our concern at the imposition of any measure which restricts our access to such capital or reduces the likelihood of its continued availability.
One important factor which I feel is often overlooked is that the amount of development capital available in Canada is limited. I am given to understand that two

projects alone, the James Bay hydro project-a venture which most of Canada and all of Quebec does not want, but will no doubt get anyway-and the Alaska pipeline project, which stands to benefit the United States, would more than exhaust the supply of domestic capital. When we consider that these are only two of many large developments to be undertaken in Canada in the near future, the obvious question to be asked before a province such as Newfoundland receives any development funds is this: What are the advantages of supplying capital to an area where the financial risk is already high?
This, then, is the shape of the Newfoundland economy. To say the least, it is not a very pleasing picture. However, it should now be clear why it would be difficult for any Newfoundlander to vote for the bill before us. Past experience has taught us that if we are to survive we cannot depend on Canadian investors and that we must, therefore, depend upon outsiders.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to take you even further away from the "Golden Triangle" to the extreme western and northern parts of our country as I make some comments on the bill and on the amendments before us.
As a small businessman and practical politician, I should like to pose this question: Why are we concerned about foreign investment? Why do we encounter a problem in this area? The answer, to my mind, having grown up in the business world and having established several business ventures, is that there simply is not enough capital in Canada to do the things that are necessary if we are to develop our potential and realise the dreams that Canadians cherish. One reason might be that there is no capital in Canada to do these things. The other reason might be that the people who control money in Canada are not willing to invest it in those areas where it does the most good. They have no faith either in the area or in the Canadian population.
It seems to me that the government can play a bigger role by telling banking and financial institutions in Canada that if they want to operate under a federal charter they should provide a service to this country. By this I mean to the whole country, not just to Toronto and Montreal, the "Golden Triangle" and highway 401. I am serious about this, Mr. Speaker. I am bothered by the fact that we have had a bill before us for the last two weeks which provides that some agency will direct foreign investment in Canada. A lot of work has been done by western Canadians to develop a dialogue with the Pacific rim countries, and they have also been expressing their anxieties at resource conferences that have been held. Some of this work, which has been done by sincere and dedicated Canadians, has been paying off in recent years, which might be one of the reasons we are so concerned today about foreign investment in Canada.
The government has realized there is a problem, and it has expressed itself by creating financial institutions like the IDB, the Farm Credit Corporation and so on. I, personally, have established several small business ventures, and on three occasions have gone to the IDB to apply for a loan for ventures in northwestern Canada. I knew that my
November 19, 1973

ideas were sound, and indeed these ventures have all paid off and are still thriving today. But on each occasion that I applied for a loan I was told, first of all, to go to my chartered bank. I went to my bank, which is the Toronto-Dominion Bank. I do not think it should be called the Toronto-Dominion Bank; it should be the Toronto Bank because it certainly has no meaningful plans for investing its money in the Dominion of Canada. I have gone to other banks and blackmailed them into helping me out with my business ideas, because invariably it takes 8, 10 or 12 months to receive an answer from the IDB.
Here am I, Mr. Speaker, a young, vigorous man who has had only 15 productive years and has no time to waste. I have already stuck out my neck and started what I thought was another really good venture. Having on three occasions applied to the IDB, I was able to tell them after some lapse of time that I had generated enough profit from my ventures that I did not need their money any more. In the last instance, the IDB wanted to sue me for the expense they had undergone in processing my loan, and this 13 months after I had applied. They wanted me to pay their solicitor's costs; they had tried to find out the colour of my grandmother's eyes and God knows what else before they could help me out with a little business venture. This is the sort of thing new development is up against, Mr. Speaker.
It is no wonder that western Canada, mid-Canada and northern Canada are in the state they are today. The Farm Credit Corporations makes loans of up to $100,000 to farmers who want to stay on the land and who want to encourage their children to stay on the land. I have a thick file concerning farmers who have sons who have expressed a willingness to stay on the land. But we do not have any faith in our farming community, their ability to clear the land with the modern means that are available and to do something worth while. This is why we are afraid of foreign investment. Foreigners who have overdeveloped and over-populated their own country look to Canada with feelings of envy, and also with a certain amount of disgust because of the way we have managed our affairs. Governments in this country-and I mean provincial as well as federal-have no faith in our people, and this is why we have a foreign investment problem.
People from the Pacific rim countries are looking to Canada today to provide some of the commodities, such as energy and lately food, which are in short supply in the world today. They are travelling around northern and western Canada assessing the potentials that exist. Certainly, they can see the potential much better than the federal government, and they are willing to lend us money to develop this potential. All they want in return is a share of the market.
It seems to me that all we need to do is to control the amount of investment that we allow to be put into each individual venture. We should also have some control over where the profits from such ventures are reinvested. Certainly, this would make sense to me. But quite frankly, I do not have faith in this government, because it has not demonstrated to me that if it were given the power of veto any significant benefit from foreign investment would occur. These profits might well be spread along highway 401 again, or used in the "golden triangle", or in the
Foreign Investment Review Act building of more concrete monsters in our large cities, while the government continues to forget that there is a back country on which Canada has to build its future. If the government had not failed to provide access roads to the resources of our vast undeveloped regions, more Canadians would have been interested in developing these resources. I suggest we are over-playing this foreign investment business, just as sometimes we overplay all this business about the ecology and the environment.
This reminds me of the story of the gardener who was visited by his priest. He was very diligently hoeing the potatoes and tending the rhubarb, and the priest, who had not seen the farmer in church for a long time, said to him: "Isn't it wonderful what one can do in co-ordination with the Lord? This wonderful garden is here and you and the Lord did it all". So the farmer said to the priest: "Yes, isn't it wonderful, but you should have seen the mess this bloody place was in when the Lord had to look after it himself"!
In British Columbia there are vast timber resources that are over-mature. Thousands of square miles have been burnt up because there were no access roads to enable us to fight fires started by lightning. The timber is overmature and will never be any good to anyone. We are harvesting only about 40 per cent of the timber resources of British Columbia; the rest is rotting away simply because Canadians do not have the faith to invest in their own country. Some of my colleagues sometimes ask for controls on lumber exports to the United States. They want tariffs imposed and more stringent controls. I say that is ridiculous. What we need is money to develop our vast timber resources that we are leaving to spoil.
I should like, for the benefit of the minister, to quote a statement made in response to an invitation by the Edmonton Journal to political and business leaders throughout Canada. I see the minister is not listening, but I should like to put on the record a statement made by one of his colleagues, which is the reason I refer to it.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: We are also afraid that the minister will not be listening once this bill is passed.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
That is right. The statement was made by Izzy Asper in the province of Manitoba. He said:
Manitoba and other western provinces have lived under a system of economic colonialism to eastern Canada for over 100 years and this cannot be allowed to continue.
Then he went on to say this:
Eastern Canada is an industrial community and has demanded, and obtained, various policies of economic protection from the federal government, from protective tariffs to restricted foreign investment. These policies are very restrictive to the development of the Western economy which is natural-resource-based and depends on world markets, free trade and large amounts of capital investment, the latter of which is largely foreign in nature due to the reluctance of the Eastern financial centres to actively promote Western investment.
During the Western resource conference, the premiers of the provinces told the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) what they thought. All the premiers of the western provinces are Canadian nationalists. What they have said is: "Do not give us any more of your handouts, any more of your

November 19, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act financial institutions to help development in the west; just leave us alone, let us incorporate and establish some of our own financial institutions so that we can play the role western Canada should play in Canadian unity and Canadian nationalism". But the message has reached deaf ears. There has been no response from this government. Sure, they were told they could own 10 per cent of a bank, but where on earth can one establish that kind of institution with that kind of faith in the future of Canada, particularly the future of our northern territories.
When I speak about the lack of faith we have in our population it reminds me of a little story I should like to tell, although I am straying a little from the subject we are discussing. I know a man named Dan Reagan from Prince George, British Columbia. He came to me with an idea he had. It is not an entirely new idea but he has perfected it to some extent. He says he has invented a new type of energy. Scientists have played with this idea for hundreds of years, but he now has a little generator operating at Prince George, British Columbia, right here in Canada. It sits on a table. I watched it operate. All it takes to light a series of light bulbs at the end of this little generator is a continuous flow of sea water. What he has done is not new. Hydrogen can be extracted from any kind of water. He controls the molecular movement in sea water or any other water. He arrests the energy generated. He advances the movement of the molecules and arrests and harnesses the energy generated by this movement. I was terribly excited about this and said that it was a big deal. I told him I wished to take it to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) in Ottawa and tell our people here that this was an idea which might become something.
I advised the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources about this idea. I told him that Dan Reagan is a man of moderate means who has an investment of a lifetime in this little generator. I told the minister I would like to have Dan Reagan travel to Ottawa and bring his generator here. For this purpose I asked the Minister if he would advance $500 to bring Dan Reagan down here so that we could set up the little generator somewhere in his office and he could see for himself how it works. The minister asked me to leave the idea with him and said that he would get back to me on the matter. One of his underlings came back to me and told me they had checked it out with some of their scientists who said it was balderdash and could not be done. It cannot be done because it is not in the books. It cannot be in the books, otherwise we would not be using other types of energy. If the scientists had said it could be done, they would have had to admit to being stupid, otherwise why would they not have done it. So, the minister is not about to give me $500 to bring Dan Reagan to Ottawa.
However, Dan Reagan will soon be on his way to Japan. He will have the patent papers in his brief case. He has the invention registered with the patent office. This cost him $300. This was not federal money or provincial money; it was his own money and the money of a few other idiots like myself who backed him. The federal government was gracious enough to lock his invention in the safe. Today, he has his generator locked up in a little trunk and he will have an all-expenses paid trip to Japan. The Japanese are interested in this invention. They should be, as should

many other people. But our government is not interested in it. We have no faith in people.
When we recall other inventors, we realize that in their time they were all considered to be idiots. I know the Japanese and the Americans will come up with another source of energy, and we will take the back seat as we always do. This is an example of the lack of faith in our own country to which I referred, and the lack of faith in our own people. I am very much afraid that those people who have directed the investments of our financial institutions throughout this land over the last 100 years will now again be called upon to tell us where in Canada the need is for investment, and where it will be of the most significant benefit to Canadians. I am very much concerned that the answer will be that it be not in mid-Canada, northern or western Canada but where the financial institutions like to invest their money, that is closest to their front door so they do not have to worry about all the other things which are happening.
Canadian banks have never made a bad loan in Canada in 100 years. When I talk about this I get angry, and I often say if we could sell our Canadian banks to the Americans it would take us less than five years to buy back our country because of the way these banking institutions operate. The money would be made available to Canadians to live their dream and do the things they cannot do because they are hampered by these idiotic policies. The government should say to these institutions that if they wish to operate under federal charter they must make loans available where they are really needed. I hope the minister will realize that we from western Canada are very unhappy, that we must be assured we will have an opportunity to have our say and to demonstrate that investment made in western, mid-and northern Canada would be of significant benefit in respect of the future of our nation. Unless the minister gets this message, I expect there will be all kinds of problems for my colleagues in northern and western Canada.

speechtext:
Motions Nos. 9 and 10 are basically very simple. Their purpose is just to increase the fines if someone knowingly breaks the law. Motion No. 9, the first motion, is to increase the fine. As the law is now written, a person who is guilty of failing to give notice on a proposed investment is liable to a fine not exceeding $5,000. It seems to me that a fine of such low magnitude is quite an insult, rather a laugh. The motion I am proposing is that the fine be increased to $100,000, which I think is more in keeping with what it should be if someone breaks the law as enacted by Bill C-132. If someone makes an investment and takes over a Canadian corporation without adhering to the regulations as outlined in the bill, and if he is the president of a huge corporation such as General Motors, a fine of only $5,000, in my view, makes a mockery of this law. It seems to me that if we do have a fine of that sort written into the law, we are accepting what amounts to a double standard, one for the rich and one for the poor. Even though it may appear to be a small thing, for some people in our society it makes some parts of the law, and some parts of the activities of this House a laughing matter.
The second amendment I am moving is similar to the first one. For failure to comply with the regulations there is a jail term which does not exceed six months. My amendment is to change the six months to one year. Again I think it makes the penalties a bit more realistic. In some cases six months may not be long enough. I believe it would be much more reflective of the opinion of hon. members if we changed this to one year. Basically, that is the purpose of the motions, to make the fines more realistic, increasing them from a maximum of $5,000 to a maximum of $100,000 and increasing the maximum jail term from six months to one year. I appeal to all hon. members to support them. They are realistic, and will make the bill more realistic. Symbolically it is important, when we talk about justice in our country, that it be seen that justice apply equally to ordinary citizens and to those who have a lot of money.

speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say one or two things with respect to the two amendments before us. I appreciate the concern of the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) that there be sufficient sanctions in this bill to ensure compliance with respect to the provisions of the bill as enacted in accordance with the wishes
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Laniel)]
of the people of Canada, expressed through their representative in parliament. But having said this, I suggest there are built-in sanctions in the bill which, I would argue, have the effect of providing sufficient inducements to compliance.
On the surface the amendments would make the penalties more severe in order to further the intentions of the bill. There would be increased fines for failure to notify the minister of a reviewable transaction. However, the real remedies in the bill are to be found in clauses 19 and 20. I would refer hon. members to those clauses, starting on page 31.
Clause 19 enables the minister to apply for a court order enjoining an investor who has failed to notify concerning a reviewable acquisition, or the setting up of a new business, from taking any particular actions which would prejudice the courts from acting under clause 20. Clause 20 permits the courts, on application from the minister, to make such orders as may be required to render an investment nugatory. This can include the courts ordering the doing of the following things-and these are the particular penalties which I think will ensure compliance with the bill's provisions, and which will have a greater effect than the penalties the hon. member is proposing: First, the revocation or suspension of voting rights attached to the shares of a corporation; second, the disposition by any person of any shares of a corporation acquired by him; and, third, the disposition by suspension of any property acquired by him that is or was used in carrying on a business. Failure to comply with an order from the courts would, in turn, allow the courts to punish for contempt of court.
I submit that these built-in sanctions, as well as those in clause 24(1) and (2) which the hon. member seeks to amend, are sufficient. For these reasons I submit that the amendments are not necessary to toughen the penalties.

He said: Mr. Speaker, very briefly this is a housekeeping or draftsmanship type of amendment. Perhaps it is not all that significant. What it proposes to do is take away a redundant sort of situation where if a person, I suggest, clearly contravenes the legislation, the question should not arise as to whether or not a corporation with which he had some prior involvement was or was not prosecuted. subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES

Mr. Speaker, I would agree with the hon. member that this is a technical question, but the advice that I have received on this technical matter is that there is an important distinction in the paragraph as it is presently worded, and I would just like to review that with hon. members.
The words "whether or not the corporation has been prosecuted or convicted therefor", which are the words which the hon. member would delete in the last sentence of clause 27, are included in order to give notice that the government reserves the right to decide whether it would be worth while to prosecute the corporation for the offence, and that our right of action respecting the corporation is a matter completely separate and apart from our right of action against the officers, directors and agents of such corporation.
Mr. Speaker, I think that those are important distinctions, and I think they are not redundant nor irrelevant to the operation of the bill and this particular section.

speakeroldname: Mr. Elmer M. MacKay (Central Nova) moved:
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
That Bill C-132, an act to provide for the review and assessment of acquisitions of control of Canadian business enterprises by certain persons and of the establishment of new businesses in Canada by certain persons, be amended in clause 30 by striking out the words "as soon as possible" in lines 4 and 5 at page 38 and substituting therefor the following:
"within sixty days".
He said: Mr. Speaker, the effect of this amendment is to indicate that we in our party are not satisfied with the rather imprecise terminology of this particular clause. I do not know for example how one defines "as soon "as possible". I do not know how one distinguishes that with any certainty in a court of law and, perhaps more important, I am not sure how one would define it with any certainty in the court of parliament.
I have reason to believe that there is a certain sympathy for this on the other side, and that the minister is prepared to consider inserting some finite time rather than leaving it on the basis of "as soon as possible", thus leaving the phrase open to the interpretation, "when it is convenient" or "when we get around to it we will do something". I do not think that is a very good situation and such a possibility should not be left in the statutes of Canada. I do not think that provision should appear in a piece of legislation which, to some extent, is a landmark in legislation pertaining to the control of foreign investment.
I do not like to take an unreasonable or narrow interpretation of what definite, finite period should be put in there. It has been suggested that because of administrative complexities 60 days is not reasonable and, of course, I have to be guided to a large extent by the experience of the minister and those who have had administrative experience. However, Mr. Speaker, I still feel that there should be some period of time specified that will guarantee that parliament and the people of Canada will get an answer and a course of action.
One of my colleagues intends to speak to this proposition and possibly propose an amendment which will provide for a period of time in excess of that envisaged in motion No. 12. On that basis, I do not feel that I should take up the time of the House, except to reiterate that some finite period of time should be inserted to substitute for this vague term "as soon as possible".

Mr. Speaker, I would certainly argue that it is not substantive in the sense you have suggested. First of all, the government proposes that a report be filed; that is within the context of the bill as presented to the House. My hon. friend suggested an amendment that, rather than give the government open season and allow the government to take all the time it wished for filing a report and making information available to the House and to the country, some specific time limit be applied, this for the obvious reason that the regional wording was far too indefinite and consequently really put no pressure on the government whatsoever in order to get about the necessary work of preparing a report to parliament and to the Canadian people. So, the subamendment is related specifically to the government's original proposal.
It would be difficult to argue that the amendment was substantive, in the normal sense of that word. Consequently, it would be equally difficult to argue that my amendment to the amendment is substantive. It is relevant to this particular clause of the bill being considered, and is relevant in the sense that it offers what the government might consider as a more reasonable period of time in order to prepare and print the documents necessary to be placed before the House. To suggest that substituting six months for 60 days, in a clause which already requires the government to prepare and table at its convenience a report, is substantive would give the word "substantive" a meaning which it does not ordinarily have.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to comment on the amendment now that it has been ruled in order. Quite frankly, there were discussions among members of various parties with respect to the wording of the clause, particularly the words "as soon as possible".
Hon. members from both sides of the House know I was prepared to accept some substitution of those words because I, too, agreed it would be very useful to have a
Foreign Investment Review Act finite time. In other words, the will of parliament will be better preserved if we insist that the report be submitted within a specific period of time.
I was concerned about the original amendment "within sixty days". Clearly, that is an impracticable objective, laudable as it may be in terms of wanting to get a full report from the new agency or commissioner. In my mind, it is simply a question of what is a practical solution in the sense of a compromise between "as soon as possible" on the one hand, which provides maximum administrative flexibility and, on the other hand, the eagerness on the part of parliamentarians to receive the account of the foreign investment review agency. I do not think there is any magic figure. I think the technique that has been adopted in the past is good. That is to say the legislation respecting the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce requires that the minister shall, on or before the 31st day of January next following the end of each fiscal year or, if parliament is not then sitting on any of the first five days next thereafter that parliament is sitting, submit to parliament a report showing the operations of the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce for that fiscal year.
That language is in the bill. My department operates under that legislation as do the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the Department of Supply and Services. In effect, that particular legislation provides 10 months for the departments to submit their annual reports to parliament. The subamendment to the amendment, which would require that the report be made in 180 days, shortens that period of time from 10 months to six months.
I am prepared to accept it because it provides for a finite period. It may be on the tight side, but that will be the problem of a new agency to organize its affairs to provide a report to parliament. I accept the amendment because we on this side are anxious to have the foreign investment review agency play a very important part in the future development of this country. For that reason, I think it important that this report be placed before parliament as soon as it is administratively possible to do so.
I cannot help but observe that in moving the subamendment, the hon. member is not joined by all members on his side in wishing to have a report placed before parliament on such an urgent basis. From listening to some, it certainly appears they would prefer that this bill not be passed. However, I recognize there are a number of members on the other side who wish to see this act passed and see it work. For that reason, I am prepared to accept the amendment.

speechtext:
That Bill C-132, An Act to provide for the review and assessment of acquisitions of control of Canadian business enterprises by certain persons and of the establishment of new businesses in Canada by certain persons, be amended in Sub-clause 31(1) by changing the period to a comma on line 15 at page 38 and adding the following:
"such a day to be no later than 60 days after Royal Assent."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this amendment is similar in intent to the amendment we dealt with a few minutes ago in that it attempts to set a time limit. Clause 31 deals with the coming into force of the legislation presently before us. At present, the date is left open to be fixed later by proclamation. I am concerned lest the minister, for one

reason or another, should choose not to have part of the act proclaimed for several months or even for several years. Or, should part of the act be proclaimed almost immediately, proclamation of the other part might be delayed for a year or two. I wanted to set a time limit, and my amendment therefore says that the date of proclamation shall be not later than 60 days after Royal Assent.
After consulting with a number of people I realise, now, that 60 days is probably too short a period; is would not give the minister sufficient time in which to draft regulations, hire staff, and so on. So, in a few moments one of my hon. friends will be moving a sub amendment extending that 60 days to six months or so. I think this would allow the minister a reasonable time in which to take all the action necessary.
I think it is important that we in this House should decide when the act is to come into force, not the minister. In my view, this is basic to the democratic process. In this way we can ensure that the act comes into force in the next six months. In the absence of such a provision, a whole series of hypothetical situations-and some might not be hypothetical-could conceivably delay the implementation of this measure. During that period all kinds of take overs and expansion into unrelated areas might take place.
So, I ask all hon. members to look seriously at clause 31 and try to reach some agreement on a definite time limitation in relation to the date on which this measure comes into force. As I said when I spoke briefly on the last amendment, I am not sure as to the precise terms of such a limitation but I strongly believe some date should be fixed so that the business community, those who are classified as non-eligible persons and the public generally, may know where they stand. This is only fair to everyone concerned. It is only democratic, and I trust the proposal I am making expresses the will of the House.

As hon. members have just heard, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) has put down an amendment requiring proclamation to be made within 60 days after Royal Assent. At present, the date is left wide open. I understand the minister feels that 60 days is too short a period. We are therefore, prepared to lengthen that period and we hope the alternative suggestion we make will be acceptable to the government and to the other parties in the House. Surely, July 1, 1974, is not an unreasonable date. Assuming that the bill is passed by the end of this month, this would give the government not just 180 days but between six months and seven months to get ready to proclaim the legislation. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent):
That Motion No. 13 be amended by deleting therefrom the words "60 days after Royal Assent" and substituting the words "July 1, 1974".
At the moment, the amendment reads: "such a date to be no later than 60 days after Royal Assent". As amended, it would read: "such a date to be no later than July 1, 1974". I trust that this revision, or compromise, will be acceptable to the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, personally, believe it is much better to set a definite date for the coming into force of that part of the bill which relates to investment than to leave the date entirely open as is presently the case.
The reasons are obvious. There are too many areas of uncertainty at the present time as far as the business world is concerned. The mere passage of the bill will open up many areas of uncertainty until such time as guidelines have been posted by the minister and test cases have been presented to the agency and the Governor in Council has ruled on them. Uncertainty will exist until a body of law is established that will give business and individuals in Canada some appreciation of exactly what this bill means and how it is going to be interpreted. To have an additional area of uncertainty as to when new investment will be covered by the bill is, I think, just one more grey area that would cause a good deal of concern. I, personally, think it is a good thing to eliminate this uncertainty by proposing a time limit, as is the case in the subamendment now before us.
Foreign Investment Review Act
It is obvious that the 60 days referred to in the original amendment was inadequate. Indeed, the hon. member who moved the amendment realized that himself. Having talked to others, he came to the conclusion that this period was quite impractical from the standpoint of administration. He realizes, as do the rest of us, that 60 days will go by before the minister even begins to put the wheels in motion. Indeed, at the end of 60 days he will be lucky to have his stationery printed and to have a few desks and other office appurtenances in place. So to expect anything more than what is basically pro forma in the first 60 days is unreasonable.
To suggest that we bring into force the second part of the act before the first part has been implemented and before guidelines have been posted would have created, if I may say so, chaos on a scale unknown probably even in the present circumstances, which is saying something, Mr. Speaker. This is why the amendment as originally framed would have had, I think, a chaotic effect. It would have produced a situation that would have been quite unacceptable and which would probably have detracted from the implementation of the bill. Rather than making it possible to move into this area smoothly and firmly, to establish precedents and a body of law which would make it possible for the minister and his officials to work efficiently and effectively to achieve the purposes set out in the bill, a great area of uncertainty would have been created which, as I say, would have prevented us from accomplishing what we want this legislation to accomplish. Therefore, we appreciate the fact that something is going to be proposed of a finite nature, which is comprehensible and understandable, and yet at the same time will give the minister a chance to give the first part of the act a reasonable shakedown cruise before the implementation of part two.
I should like to make this further appeal to the members of the NDP, who have demonstrated their sincerity in this area, to do the same thing with in regard to one of the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). These hon. gentlemen represent a party that has three provincial governments in this country. Those provincial governments, as other provincial governments, are concerned about the problem of communications that exists between the federal and provincial governments. And their concern is well founded, Mr. Speaker.
The object of the exercise is to make this bill work in such a way that we can provide alternative investment capital necessary to develop all parts of Canada. In order to do this we must have communications of a sensitive yet instant kind, a kind that has not been forthcoming in this country for quite a while. We will require the kind of communications that are just the opposite of the sort we have had recently-the confrontation type of politics we have experienced between federal and provincial governments, particularly in regard to energy matters.
If the screening agency is to be effective and we are to use the mechanism that is set up to encourage Canadians to invest more fully in their own resource and industrial development, then it is absolutely imperative that from the very outset-not at some subsequent time but at the very outset-the lines of communication between the min-

In other words, we must establish a hot line between the minister, his agency and each of the ten provinces, and indeed the territories as well. We should remember that they, too, are very directly concerned. Of all the areas of this country, there is probably no area that has more potential for development and is more concerned about obtaining adequate amounts of capital to finance that development than the two territories in the north.
Nevertheless, we do have this haunting fear regarding the lack of a time limit within which the minister must bring in his annual report. It is easy to see that wide latitude should be given. At the same time, unless there is some necessity to do something, the propensity is to find an excuse for not doing it. We now have a situation where the minister must file a report within a certain period of time. He has agreed this is a good provision and that there is pressure on him to comply. However, we also think there should be equal pressure on the minister to notify at once provinces that are affected significantly by any proposed takeover, in the first instance under the first part of the act, and then later on once the whole act has been proclaimed. What greater certainty could there be, Mr. Speaker, than having the minister and his agency required by law to consult the provinces by giving notice the instant they are advised of a particular situation coming within the ambit of the bill? We feel that this requirement is cardinal. We want a good bill, a bill that would be acceptable to all people across this country.
One could not help but be impressed this afternoon by the eloquence of those who spoke about the feeling that exists in the eastern and western regions in this country for some guarantee that the federal government will be sensitive to their real needs. Equally, one could not help but be impressed by the fact that the large amount of investment that has taken place in Newfoundland since Confederation has for the most part been from without Canada. This is not because that province would not have preferred to have Canadian investment and Canadian ownership and control, but when faced with the opportunity, Canadian entrepreneurs and financial institutions were not able to come through, and did not come through, with the necessary investment capital.
Perhaps there is a matter of insight involved in respect of those of us in central Canada who feel very strongly that we must come to grips with this problem, who feel very strongly that too much of our industry is owned outside of Canada, who feel very strongly that the trend in the future and immediately is toward greater participation in the development of our own industries and resources, and who feel very strongly that the moment of decision has come. We must also understand that people in other parts of the country feel equally strongly that their points of view be taken into account.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) is very interesting. Like the previous one, it proposes to substitute a finite time for a very indefinite state so far as the original legislative attempt is concerned. I think that most hon. members on reflection will feel this is the type of amendment that should be supported and, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) just said, one wonders at the drafting skill that brings to this House legislation worded in the way it is.
I think the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville has expressed in his amendment a real concern that no doubt has crossed the minds of many hon. members, I suppose mostly opposition members, that this government may be a little less than sincere and frank in its desire to implement the various provisions of this foreign investment review act. No doubt it is a perfectly legitimate action on the part of the government to attempt to get the very maximum political mileage out of this step to finally control foreign investment in Canada, and none of us can argue that they are not entitled to it. However, they have had an opportunity to do this for a long time. They could have taken this step in the last session of parliament, but for one reason or another it was not done. Now, having had the initiative to bring the bill before the House, one would think they would want to see the proposals implemented as soon as possible.
Certainly there is a great deal of room for speculation in this regard. Long before I became a member of the House I can remember reading in various publications about acts that were brought in which were ostensibly for the good of Canada and were to have a considerable impact on our nation, such as for example the Canada Water Act which was brought in with great fanfare. I believe it was discussed for a considerable length of time in this august chamber, and finally passed with unanimous consent. However, in my humble opinion this piece of legislation has not been very efficiently promoted or fostered by this government. There is also the Territorial Sea and Fishing Zones Act which, when it was passed by the House, afforded a great deal of comfort, in theory, at least, to Atlantic Canada.
What I am wondering-and so is, I am sure, the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville; perhaps this is part of the motivation for his amendment, apart from the excellent procedural point of instituting a finite time-is whether he is also of the opinion that this government might very well like to have the name but not the game. I am wondering whether he does not think the government needs to have some guarantee forced upon it so that it would in fact bring in the relevant provisions. I would suggest, again without being too cynical, that the government may be less than happy to act as expeditiously as some members of the opposition would like it to act.
Of course, the minister can make the point, and with some justification, that so far as provincial consultation and notice are concerned, he needs the consent of cabinet and that, even if he so wished, he will not be able to act as some sort of oriental despot who can do what he wishes

under this legislation. There are certain political realities with which he must conform.
However, I wish to take a brief moment to make a final plea to the minister, as did the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer) and the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich, and remind him that we have very real concerns in our various parts of Canada, including the territories. We hope that in considering the various ramifications of this type of legislation, the government will realize that we must have some sort of provincial consultation on the one hand and substitution of alternate forms of capitalization on the other. If some sort of attempt is not made by the government to understand this, then I fail to see how this legislation will receive the necessary acceptance and co-operation.
An objection has been made by some of my colleagues that the notice requirements, as defined by the Interpretation Act, would provide too much of an administrative burden for the government in supplying the various provincial administrations with the kind of information it would feel obliged to provide because of the definition of what "notice" may be. This is not entirely a valid argument. Surely there is some scope left to the government, and the minister does not necessarily have to follow in every literal respect the definition of "notice." Surely, with all the staff at his command, the minister would be able to provide the provinces, in some sort of summary form, the type of notice that would not be too bulky on the one hand and on the other hand would be sufficient for the provinces' interests.
There is really nothing more that needs to be said about the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville. It is a good type of amendment and should be looked at seriously. Mr. Speaker, since you may require a little time to dispose of argument and perhaps rule on amendment No. 14, I will conclude at this point.
