subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel particularly pleased and honoured this evening to see so many cabinet ministers in the House, particularly the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) who is the sponsor of this bill. It is an unusual sight at this time of the day.
This is an important piece of legislation, Mr. Speaker, not so much for what it contains, because it contains very little, but for what it does not contain in providing for the process and the mechanism by which national parks are established. It also affords members an opportunity to extol the virtues of their own areas and the beauties there and to explain why there should be national parks in areas where they do not exist at the moment.
In my initial remarks I want to point out that northern British Columbia does not contain any national parks at the moment, and therefore if I were to relate this bill just to the interests of my own area it would not really matter whether it passed or not. It would have no bearing on whether a national park is established in that area. That will come about as a result of discussions between the provincial government and the federal government and the assignment of lands and all the other matters that enter into an agreement to establish a national park.
On Friday, the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) spoke about Forillon national park. What he said had merit but I want to depart from that position. He invited all hon. members and others to take a holiday and visit Forillon to enjoy the beauties of that park when it becomes developed. I disagree with the concept that a national park has to be developed before it can be enjoyed and appreciated. I think we have gone overboard on this concept of development and I apply this to provincial parks as well. We have tended to commercialize them, make them attractive to the mobile tourist who comes along with his trailer, portable television and all the accoutrements of home to visit these parks. I am one of those who wants to see them maintained and preserved in their natural state. I think

November 19, 1973
National Parks Act
the concept of parks should be that of preservation of wilderness areas and nature, rather than an encroachment upon nature and the development of blacktop roads, hot dog stands and commercial ventures and all the other highly organized accompaniments of today's concept of national parks.
Take, for example, the Queen Charlotte Islands, particularly the west coast facing upon the expanse of the Pacific Ocean. It is difficult to get to that area because there are no roads. One has to get there by boat or aircraft . Commercial aircraft do not fly there, so it becomes a charter venture which is not really that expensive when flying from some of the communities on the Queen Charlottes themselves. The west coast is an indescribable structure. It was the home of a number of Indian communities in pre-European days. It was an area in hibernation, so to speak, in which one could gain some concept of the spiritual nature of nature itself. The mere sight of that expanse of water, its movement and its surging, and the cliffs and trees and the sea life, with the wildlife of the area, is something to be remembered and preserved and conserved. I can think of no better way of doing it than by establishing a national park for that purpose.
Just north of Terrace where I live there are some lava beds, the result of an outflow of lava from a volcano that erupted something like 400 years ago. That lava flow is reflected in the stories and history of the Nishga Indians who live along the Nass River. They tell of the plight of their forefathers three or four centuries ago when the volcano erupted, spewed lava and drove people from villages to other sites. Just north, a few hundred miles away I believe, is the only active volcano in Canada. It is not active at this time, the eruptions taking place on a cyclical pattern which ends every 300 years or thereabouts.
I know that scientists of the federal Department of Energy, Mines and Resources are near Mount Edzizq, studying the lava flows in the Grand Canyon of the Stikine River. Several volcanoes have erupted in the region. There are a number of volcanic cones in the area. The top of this mountain area is glaciated. Areas like this should be preserved and dedicated in future as nondeveloped national parks. Their preservation as national parks is something that ought to be considered.
Also, we should consider our ocean spaces as national parks. A couple of years ago, as recorded in Hansard on October 19, 1971, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Davis) spoke about what was loosely or generally referred to as an underwater or marine park in the Gulf of Georgia. Technically, it should be known as Georgia Strait; those of us who live in the area always refer to it as the Gulf of Georgia, although it is not a gulf. There is a reference in Hansard to the Minister of the Environment referring to studies and discussions taking place with the government of British Columbia about the park. Apparently, within a few weeks of October 19 there was to be a formal understanding with the province in that connection. We have heard nothing further since then.
There are a number of areas on the west coast and east coast, bordering on the ocean that should be preserved and set aside as conservation areas. In those areas people

should be able to see the beauties of undersea life. In this connection I have heard it said that national parks and other parks are valuable from the point of view of tourism and tourists. I know there is a tendency for people to extol the economic benefits that come to an area in which there is a park. They say that economic benefits come from tourists who visit those areas. A great deal of that so-called benefit is mythical. It does not come about.
Near where I live the world's largest steelhead salmon was caught in the Kispiox River, a river that is frequented by tourists. A few years ago a young lad of 18 spent four or five hours catching this fish. In the end he pulled out of the water a 92-pound spring salmon-a fantastically big fish. Let me point out that the Skeena River is one of the most important salmon spawning rivers in Canada, as is the Nass River and the whole northern area. These rivers attract tourists who come to camp and fish. Many come with self-contained campers. They bring their own gas, often in 45-gallon drums because it is cheaper that way than buying it locally. They bring their own larders stocked with food. They do not even purchase a fishing licence, very likely having bought it as soon as they crossed the border, if they are American, or in another town if they come from Canada. They leave behind relatively little in an economic sense. They leave their garbage and their litter-we provide facilities for that. The concept that tourism brings economic benefits to an area is just not true when viewed over-all.
An unfortunate situation has arisen in some of our parks, regrettably, because both federal and provincial governments have not been sure who had legislative or constitutional authority in the area. I am referring to situations in which people, primarily from the United States-I am not knocking United States citizens for this-have come with camper units and, as well, with a small canning factory. They have spent their time, say, on the Kispiox River or elsewhere and have engaged in sports fishing, which comes under the jurisdiction of the provincial government. They catch fish and can them in these mobile canning units. They clean the fish right there and then, and bottle or can them right there and then and take them back home. They catch salmon and other species of fish, sometimes for commercial purposes.
We must prevent this happening. I do not consider that where this sort of thing takes place the activity is of any great value to the area. We want to put our objection on record and say that when we are talking of developing or establishing national parks we should not do it with that concept in mind. Such activity is not necessary for people who go to a park to enjoy it.
I have some objections to the bill, Mr. Speaker. One of my objections is companion to the objection raised by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth) the other day. It has to do with the relationship between the federal government and the provinces and the federal government and the two territories. Under the bill, parks can be established or expanded in a province when there is agreement with the province. When it comes to the Yukon and Northwest Territories, no such agreement is necessary. The territorial councils are not considered even as being competent to make those decisions.
November 19, 1973

The Yukon and Northwest Territories are treated pater-nalistically in the bill. I know how much the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development detests the word "paternalism". He drags it out every time he is in a corner. The bill is paternalistic inasmuch as the section of the bill dealing with the relationships with the Yukon Territory and the Northwest Territories speaks not of agreement but of consultation. We know, from the history of this government, what it means by consultation. It does not consult for discovering what others want, or for the purpose of getting advice about something with respect to which the federal government may change its mind. With this government, consultation is merely something for providing a technical avenue by which things can be discussed so that the federal government can go ahead and do what it planned in the first place.
A couple of days ago I looked up the word "consult" in the dictionary. Perhaps the most appropriate definition that can be applied to this government is the reference that says "to consult your pillow"-in other words, to sleep on the matter or think about it in your dreams. That is the type of consultation that is involved.
Some parts of this bill have merit. Although they will have some value for simple questions, they will denigrate the position of the Yukon and Northwest Territories Councils with regard to groups to be consulted but not to reach agreement. As far as I am concerned, the bill should fail on those grounds if none other. Surely, in this enlightened day and age, with all the respect we have for levels of government and democracy, we should write into this piece of legislation with respect to the Yukon and, the Northwest Territories that the formation of parks should become a matter of agreement between the federal government and territorial governments. I hope when we get to the committee stage the appropriate amendment will be written in.
I want to talk about a gross failing in the bill. This has apparently been endorsed by the Conservative Party. At no time during the second reading debate on this bill has one iota of interest been exhibited on the subject matter of aboriginal rights of the native people of this country. The other day, in the province of Quebec, there was a Superior Court decision involving the James Bay project. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development took 275 per cent of the credit for that decision. I see the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) nodding his head and saying yes, he should. It is a shame that the hon. member is not raising the point I am going to raise with regard to this particular piece of legislation, because this carries with it a denial by the minister with regard to his concern for aboriginal rights.
If the minister and the government had that degree of concern totally and fully about respect for aboriginal rights, they would have included in this bill a clause repealing section 6 (3) of the National Parks Act. That is to be retained in the legislation; there is no thought of removing it. It is paternalistic and offensive. It should be offensive to the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo. The section reads:
The governor in council may authorize the minister-
National Parks Act
That is the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development.
-to purchase-
That carries with it the concept of a mutual agreement.
-expropriate-
That means to steal.
-or otherwise acquire any lands or interests therein, including the lands of Indians-
The minister and other members of the government say how beautiful it is that they can stand up and say they respect the fundamental right of the Indian people with regard to the land they occupy, and want to carry it forward in the statute law of this nation. I know how much the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo wants to ask questions. I know how much he is in need of information. If he would do it in a formal way when I conclude my remarks, I will do my best to respond to him. To carry forward the government's right to expropriation of Indian lands flies completely in the face of the question of aboriginal rights. I would rather not see the bill proceeded with until we had dealt with this matter.

There goes the chatterbox from Kamloops-Cariboo. If he were the type of member he should be, and stood up and fought for the rights of the Indian people, I would pay attention to him. However, he has not done that. He has not done anything. He is an apologist for a weak, insipid government on the question of aboriginal rights.
I want to deal with another section of the National Parks Act. It concerns the relationship of Indian people and Indian lands. If the minister does not expropriate Indian lands, that is, take them without consent or agreement, but acquires them by lease under another section or regulation, the minister is permitted to levy taxes against those lands even though they were not expropriated. The act contains that provision. One thing the Indian people have held dear to them as a slim recognition of aboriginal rights is freedom from taxation on the reserve except taxation that the band council may levy. The minister wants to retain the authority to expropriate those lands and levy taxes for various purposes against them. If the taxes are not paid, the minister or the government can proceed to sell the land for unpaid taxes.
If the Indian people want to stand up for their fundamental right and say that the Indian Act states their land shall not be taxed, the minister can say it shall be taxed because the National Parks Act gives him that authority. That is regardless of what the Bill of Rights may or may not say. There was an indication of that a few days ago when the Supreme Court reached the stupid decision that the Bill of Rights had no validity whatsoever in any matter. If an Indian stands up for his right and does not pay taxes, the minister can seize and sell the land for non-payment of taxes.
There is another provision in the act. All of this can flow from section 6(3) of the act which is to be retained. If the Indian people want to exercise their fundamental basic right to fish or hunt for food, the minister can say they are

November 19, 1973
National Parks Act
in violation of a provision of the act because the regulations prohibit that, even though that is characteristic of the whole history of concern about aboriginal rights. It is easily understood; everyone has heard about it. There have been a great number of cases on this. If an Indian exercised his aboriginal right to catch fish, the minister could seek a conviction. The person would be liable to a fine of up to $500 and up to six months in jail if convicted.
If an Indian person decides to exercise his aboriginal right to fish and to hunt, which Indian people have done from time to time, this is their inherited right, something that was not taken away from them by treaty. If this is so, any park warden or any constable can without warrant or other legal process enter and search any building, structure, boat, vehicle, etc. In other words, mere suspicion on the part of a park warden could carry with it the authority to break into people's homes at any time of the day or night, within the park or outside the park, with respect to timber, minerals, hay, birds, fish, mammals-the latter being part of the way of life of the Indian people. And these powers are to be continued in the act.
As far as I can see, there is no provision in this bill which affects this right which the minister wishes to keep, namely, the right to expropriate Indian lands, to levy taxes against those lands and to sell them in the event the taxes are not paid, even though taxes may have been withheld on grounds of principle. All this, together with provisions for laying charges, imposing terms of imprisonment up to six months, and so on, is carried forward in the legislation as constituting authority which the minister wishes to keep. In my view this is contrary to what we should be doing in this House.
I have no great objection to what is contained in this bill, though I do have doubts about some aspects and I disagree with the position accorded to the Councils of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories inasmuch as they are not allowed any measure of real participation in making decisions about national parks. However, I do take strong and serious objection to the provisions which are allowed to remain in the act. For the life of me, I cannot understand why the minister should wish to retain those provisions, especially since he has been consistent, in the last few months anyway, in his statements about aboriginal rights.
All I can conclude is that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has more to say in these matters than the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. We all recall the position taken by the Prime Minister in September, 1969, when he said in Vancouver that as far as he was concerned the Indian people did not have any Indian rights; the government rejected that concept. The same view was expressed on a number of occasions, and it was only changed when the Supreme Court of Canada rendered its decision in the Nishga case. Then the Prime Minister said, "Well, we did not think you had any aboriginal rights, but maybe you have some legal rights, whatever they are." He did not seek to clarify what those rights might be.
So either the provision giving the minister the right to take Indian lands, and the imposition of taxes and all the

invasion of property which goes therewith is retained in the act as a result of an oversight on the part of the minister-and I cannot take this possibility very seriously-or it is retained in the act because basically the government has no regard for aboriginal rights. Oh, ministers will pay homage to those rights when they are won by somebody else in a court, but when it comes to action, to doing something about them seriously, the answer is, no Sir. What other reasons could there be for retaining in this day and age a provision which says that a cabinet minister has the right to expropriate Indian lands?
Let us talk about the Northwest Territories. Here there are no surrendered lands; all the land belongs, in an historical sense, to the Indian people. Yet all the government is prepared to do is to consult with the Council of the Northwest Territories, without regard to the people native to the area, without regard to their historic claims, without regard to the fact that the whole of the Northwest Territories in an historic sense comes within the domain of the people native to that area. This is also the case in my own part of British Columbia. Yet here again is an area in which the minister wishes to retain the right to expropriate Indian lands. And with respect to those areas in which he is the sole commander-in-chief he does not even want to enter into an agreement with the elected council of the territory but simply to engage in consultation.
I also object to the manner in which the bill reached us. My views about the Senate and its facility or opportunity to deal with matters of a public nature are well known. I think that a great many senators do not represent people; they represent money, banks, oil companies and the rapacious capitalists in this nation. They represent the interests of the multinational corporations as opposed to the interests of the Canadian public. Today we are considering a piece of legislation which I believe ought not to have originated in the Senate because it deals with the fundamental interests of human beings. Perhaps we should make a start in this parliament on a bill denying the Senate the right to look at legislation which fundamentally affects the rights of human beings.
At one time the Senate did have a function to perform. It used to pass on divorce cases from Quebec and Newfoundland. Quite appropriate, I thought. But parliament took that function away. The Senate used to deal with private bills to establish corporations, insurance companies, and so on. Those bills used to originate in the Senate, quite properly, I thought, because the Senate represents those interests. However, as a result of a series of objections by some of us in this chamber, that authority too was removed from the Senate. Now such incorporations or changes take place by the letters patent process.
The Senate only had two opportunities to do anything worth while. One was to deal with divorce and the other was the incorporation of insurance and finance companies. They were removed. What has probably occurred is that the Senate, realizing how useless it was becoming, recognizing what has always been the fact, has implored the government to give it something to do. Therefore the minister went to his old friend, Paul Martin, and said, "Senator Paul, I have a bill that is designed to keep intact
November 19, 1973

in my hands the right to take away Indian lands, and I want to keep that right. If I bring the bill into the House early in the session"-and I point out that it was introduced in the Senate on March 27 of this year-"those guys in the Commons and those intransigent people in the Indian affairs and northern development committee will tear me to shreds. So how about you, an old friend of the people, introducing the bill in the Senate? In that way it will proceed through and no one will even know it is there. The public will pay no attention to it, there will be no press about it, and it will sneak through. Then we will bring it into the Commons in the last days before the Christmas recess when people are interested in other important matters, slip it through and no one will know the difference. Plus the fact that it will look like you guys over there are doing something".
After all, Mr. Speaker, this is Bill S-4, and bills are dealt with in the order they are introduced. Bill S-l was the traditional, respectful piece of legislation which was not designed to go anywhere but just maintains tradition. What Bills S-2 and S-3 are, I have no idea.

Mr. Speaker, my first intention in rising and taking part in this debate was not to defend the Senate against the attacks that have just been directed at it. But I find myself compelled, for the second time in two days, to pay tribute to some efforts that were made by the other place.
I had the opportunity last Friday to take part in the debate on the joint declaration that had been issued after the visit of the European Parliament that had been arranged by the joint Senate committee and tonight I rise in a debate which deals with a bill coming from the other place.
However, this is not my only interest in this bill, as you will probably see in my remarks. The constituency I represent is very suitable for the establishment of a park. Besides, after I was elected, in 1970, I stood as champion of the establishment of such a park in the northern part of my constituency. And at that time, Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec had just agreed, after hesitating for years, to admit the principle of the establishment of a park in the Gaspe Peninsula, and another one in the St. Maurice Valley.
My other interest is to take the defence-though he is very clever to defend himself-of the minister responsible for Indian affairs, because I had the opportunity, during the La Macaza title transfer on January 10, with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister who was with me, to find out, to really understand the minister's popularity among the Indian people of this country.
Mr. Speaker, most of the Indian leaders of the province of Quebec whom I saw during the ceremony have praised
7938

November 19, 1973
National Parks Act
the minister on several occasions. Unfortunately, he was recovering from that unfortunate illness which kept him away from the House for several months. On that occasion, the Quebec Indian chiefs repeated over and over again how much he was appreciated, how the Indians recognized his efforts, his eagerness and his steadfastness to improve their living conditions, act as their spokesman and the champion of their interests throughout the country.
Mr. Speaker, we saw his first reaction when he learned the judgment of the court on the James Bay issues. He immediately upheld the interests of the Indians and I think that the native people are grateful and have not missed, on various occasions and not only when I was in La Macaza, to show their attachment and their admiration for everything he has done for them.
As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, right after my election to this House, most municipalities in my riding made representations to me seeking from this government with the agreement of the province of Quebec the establishment of a national park in the northern part of my riding, that is in the uninhabited area situated north of Chute-Saint-Phillipe and Val-Viger, east of Mont-Laurier, stretching towards Abitibi in the north-west for about a hundred miles. This conforms well with the character of people of this area and those situated a little further to the south because for years the riding I represent distinguished itself by the way it welcomes tourists, making tourism its industry.
There is a long-established tradition and the people of that are conscious of having a special vocation for that industry. The people in my riding, in that area at least, could very well guarantee the success of such a project, enabling the more than two million people in Greater Montreal to get closer to nature, to the mountains we find in my riding, to the magnificent lakes and rivers and also take advantage of that greenery that is found almost everywhere in the constituency, and all the more as the building of the Sainte-Scholastique or Mirabel airport, whether we want it or not, will mean a very important increase in population during the next decade.
That move is already being felt months after months. The real estate agents in that part of my constituency, in the lower Laurentians talk again and again about the interest generated by the building of the airport.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the establishment of new provincial parks, especially in that central part of the province of Quebec, is a must. The development of Forillon National Park was excellent news in 1968 or 1969 and I could say that the development of St. Maurice Park is excellent news for the people of the province of Quebec, for it will be as beautiful as Forillon Park, but it is not as readily accessible to the Greater Montreal area as a park in the northern part of my constituency would be.
I estimate it would take beween seven and nine hours to travel from Montreal to Forillon, while the area I refer to, which is north of Montreal, could be reached within two hours. Access to that oasis could thus be made much easier and much more regular.
When Forillon Park was being created, Mr. Speaker, following long-I should say too long-negotiations with

Quebec authorities, it was a result of pressures exercised by the people of the province who were asking for the establishment of national parks which could rival in beauty with those in the western provinces. They had been asking for these parks for years.
Finally, the provincial government of the time became sensible and gave in to the pressures or requests from the people of Quebec. However, we are still in the red considering the number of national parks which are found in Alberta, for instance, or in other western provinces, compared with the number that we have now in Quebec.
If you except the Plains of Abraham which, in my view, are much more a park of a special nature than a national park, I would say that both parks, St. Maurice and Forillon, will not meet the demand and requirements of the Quebec people.
It is true that today the number of national parks has nearly doubled compared with what it was ten years ago, thanks to the initiative and tenacity of the minister responsible. Not so long ago, he said that by the year 2,000, Canada should have at least 60 parks.
Who will profit from the facilities offered in these parks, Mr. Speaker? First, the population of Canada, and then the tourists who come to visit us each year from Europe or the United States. For several decades, people in North America, in Canada and the United States have gone to Europe, to the lands of their ancestors.
Now the European economy is allowing people from Europe to come to North America and visit this new land which has attracted so many of their sons. One finds, of course, a great many cousins in North America, both French-speaking and English-speaking, and of other ethnic origins represented in this country as well.
Since the European economy reached our level you can rest assured that Europeans with the easy means of communication available today will also want to enjoy our beautiful national parks, our beautiful rivers and lakes.
Surely those people will enjoy them as well as Canadians from all parts of this country who will soon enjoy a 38 hour week and undoubtedly a 36, 34 or 32 hour week would mean a work week consisting of barely four days of eight hours each.
All people, especially workers, do not have the means to buy a lot on the shore of a lake and enjoy the beauty of nature that can be found in the Laurentians. It will be pressingly urgent to set up facilities so they can drive their habitat with them, whether it be a trailer-tent, or ordinary tent, a trailer or a motor home and enjoy, as those well off, the beauty of nature and the pure air the Laurentians and a national park can offer them.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, before the province of Quebec catches up with some provinces in this country in terms of the number of parks several years will have gone by. However, I come back charging with the will of the representatives of city councils in my riding who in 1971 and early in 1972 asked that a park be set up in the northern part of my riding. Economically speaking, Mr. Speaker, it has become excessively difficult to interest industry in the private sector in coming down to that part of the province
November 19, 1973

of Quebec which, under certain aspects, is still underdevelopped.
In my opinion it could be illegal to shift tertiary industry to this area when we think of the damages which the presence of heavy industries could cause to the environment. Because of the aptitude already shown by the population, because also of the sites and the facilities available, the establishment of a park in that part of the province would surely be welcome and would help create employment, thus ensuring the financial security of the people in that sector of my constituency.
Just the same I would like, before ending my remarks, Mr. Speaker, to deal with a few clauses of the bill, particularly with the one conferring to federal authorities the power to regulate or to apply traffic regulations on these lands, to enforce regulations and laws. Moreover, Bill S-4 will enable the Canadian government to amalgamate or to add to existing national parks lands which our country already owns.
Clause 9 of the bill specifies the boundaries and description of Forillon National Park. From the description of this park, in the Gaspe area in the eastern part of the province, it can be seen that this very beautiful park the equal of those established in western Canada, covers an area of 60,000 acres or 92,805 square miles.
We welcome such measures. The Quebec population is delighted at the decision of provincial authorities to yield to popular demands for the establishment of national parks. However, I am convinced that the population is not satisfied yet. During a campaign I started in 1971-72 for the creation of a park in my constituency, municipal councils were unanimous in calling for the creation of a new park at the northern end of the constituency of Labelle.
Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity to repeat to the minister that popular interest for this project is very much alive in my constituency.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this measure because I think that in referring the bill to the committee for study we will have an opportunity to examine in some detail the policy of this government toward the national parks and the national park system. One of the reasons I am particularly interested in this subject is the fact that although the government seems to have evolved a national parks policy, I submit that on the face of it the parks policy cannot work to the same degree in all national parks.
If I may, I would like to use as a prime example the national park in my own riding. The reason I use this park as an example is that although it is a famous park, it is probably the smallest national park in Canada. I have listened with a great deal of interest to hon. members who preceded me speaking of national parks of hundreds of thousands of acres and thousands of square miles in area. The park of which I speak, the Point Pelee national park, could be placed in one of the lakes of one of the Canadian national parks. Its area is less than that of the townsites found in the Canadian national parks.
Why is there concern about the policy? One should know something of the history of the Point Pelee national
National Parks Act
park to understand why there is a great deal of concern about the policy of this government with regard to national parks. That park is particularly noteworthy because it comprises the most southern part of this country, with the exception of Pelee Island lying in Lake Erie. Point Pelee national park is located as far south along the longtitude running through the city of New York and the parallel from New York to the northern part of the state of California. When you are standing in that particular park you are south of one-third of the population of the United States.
Because of this location, the forest, the fauna and the ecology of the park are unique in Canada. There are trees and plants to be found there that are not found in other parts of Canada, and there are birds there that are not to be found in any other part of Canada. It is the migration point of many of the birds in their migratory flight from the southern hemisphere to the north. Where else would you find butterfly trees? For those who are not familiar with butterfly trees, let me explain that these are trees which in the fall of the year are almost covered in their entirety with Monarch butterflies which rest there before migrating south across Lake Erie. Hundreds of tourists travel to that particular area to see this unique display.
This park has not always been a national park. It is comprised of some farmland, marshland and wooded land. The farmers there grew various crops, first grain crops and then specialized crops such as asparagus. There were apple orchards, and because of the particular nature of the point where the flow of the east and west part of Lake Erie come together with a vicious undertow, it was necessary in the early days to establish a lifeguard station. The lifeguards performed yeoman service, saving many lives. Even today it is necessary to patrol the beaches, which are unique for their very fine sand and are a great attraction to tourists, because they can be very dangerous owing to the undertow where the two bodies of water flow together.
The policy of this government with regard to the park went awry because the local citizens, municipal and township councils there were not taken into confidence by the government and had no idea what the government was attempting to do with the park. They just found that suddenly the normal use of the park was curtailed, and they were somewhat mystified as to what the government was proposing to do.
No doubt the government's policy in trying to preserve that park in its natural state was an admirable one. However, it must not be forgotten that throughout the years the park had evolved together with the community. Camps for boys and girls had been set up on an alternate basis. There were picnic grounds for family picnics and church picnics. This was part of the community. The park was an attraction for thousands and thousands of tourists, and as a result a tourist industry was developed all along the approaches to the park. Restaurants cropped up and cottages were built. The park became part of the community. Because it was a focal point for tourists, the area attracted hundreds of thousands of dollars each year for the people of the community.
Now, all of a sudden, because of the national parks policy, this is changed. The number of cars going into the park was curtailed, the parking areas were reduced, no
7940

November 19, 1973
National Parks Act
new leases were granted to householders and no new camps were established in the park. The roadways were curtailed to traffic, and traffic was stopped at the main gate in the main part of the park. A train was introduced to take people through the park. Bird walks were established and so were trails through the park.
This is all very fine, but it changed the whole complexion of the park. Right beside the park there was an extensive marsh. An additional problem was created because all of a sudden hunters were told they could no longer hunt ducks in that marsh. This might appear to be commendable, but let me point out that the ban disrupted the community because in the original deed of that area hunters were granted the right to hunt in the park. The hunters did not go to the park for the sake of shooting only. Throughout the years hunters have carefully taken in thousands of bushels of grain to feed to the ducks. When hunting they were careful to make sure that a sufficient number of birds was left to ensure the continuation of the species. They were careful enough to see that the flocks did not grow so large as to become a nuisance to the surrounding farmlands. That was one problem caused by the marsh.
A second problem caused by this extensive marsh was that it was adjacent to diked farmland and more than once water broke through from the marsh and inundated the farmland. There was constant questioning about who should maintain the dikes, the farmers, the provincial government or the federal government, and always the answer came back that it was the federal government's responsibility because this was a national park. The national policy did not allow for sufficient consultation between those who actually knew the park and the administrators in Ottawa, hundreds of miles away. In fact, we would have had more chaos had it not been for the park administrators sent to the area. Fortunately, they had an understanding of what the government wanted to do, as well as a real appreciation of the feelings of the people of the area.
One bone of contention between the administration and the local people was a child's camp in that park. It was established under an estate legacy. A board of administrators was set up and took children from all the surrounding communities on a rotational basis. Groups of girls and boys were carefully supervised during their time at the camp. They walked forest trails, saw the beauty of nature and swam in the lakes. Most were city children who would not have an opportunity to go to other camps. But the national parks policy changed all that. The administration closed down the camp, and had it not been for the intervention of local citizens who were very wrought up about the matter, and finally the acquiescence of the minister himself, that park would have been closed to the children.
It is all very well to keep parks in their natural state for future genera' ions, but surely the people and children of today have some rights. They must have some place to go. Reason must prevail. We should not shut out everybody in order to make plans for tomorrow. This is why I am interested in this bill, and it is why I hope when it goes to committee we will have an opportunity to inquire into the government's plans for the various national parks. Policies 
for national parks which encompass hundreds of thousands of acres may not be suitable for national parks that encompass only a few acres. My plea to the government today is that it take another look at park policies which encompass parks of totally different natures.
In my area, national parks are very scarce. Hundreds of thousands of people there would have to travel many, many miles to reach another national park. For them, Point Pelee national park has been an oasis for years, and it would be very sad if policies conceived by parliament and administered by Ottawa terminated the pleasure that local communities have enjoyed when using that national park. The local citizens are very proud of Point Pelee national park. Since they have a vested interest and are so proud of the park, it is only fair they should have some say in how the park is administered.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my participation in this debate may be questioned by some who wonder why I should bother to speak about national parks since there are none in my riding. I would point out that the constituency of Moncton is situated halfway between the two national parks which presently exist in New Brunswick. Because many of my constituents enjoy the facilities of these parks and because Moncton, being the transportation centre of the Maritimes, is traversed by everyone who visits the parks, I have a very special interest in them. It is true, as the parliamentary secretary said, that this bill is merely a housekeeping bill, particularly concerned with updating the administration. I am particularly interested in clause 2 which gives the governor in council power to extend the boundaries and incorporate Crown lands within existing national parks.
I have mentioned that there are two national parks in New Brunswick. The problem of expansion is not too critical in the Kouchibouguac national park. It is a new park and the government is still upgrading facilities there. Therefore I shall confine my remarks to Fundy national park. The hon. member who preceded me said that the national park in his area is the smallest in Canada. I cannot argue with that; but if Fundy is not the second smallest, it certainly is one of the smallest. It is about 80 square miles in extent. Although small, it is one of the most beautiful parks in Canada. Visitors who have been there will confirm this. It contains some of the most beautiful scenery in Atlantic Canada, sea line, rugged forest and mountain lines. It is one of the real beauty spots. The problem at Fundy is simply that the park is too popular. Maybe that is not quite the proper way to put it. Anyway, it is so popular that it is now completely overcrowded.
In 1948, when the decision was made to develop Fundy national park, there were very few roads in there. Being a pretty rugged sector of the country, it attracted few visitors except campers and prospectors. The popularity of the park has steadily increased since then and I can give some figures in support of that. It is said that attendance at our national parks has doubled in each decade from 1952 to 1972. Fundy national park was officially opened in July, 1950, and in the year 66,300 visitors went there. By 1970, this had increased to 640,000 visitors. I have not seen the figures for 1972, but I venture to say they are over 700,000 and perhaps close to 800,000. The reason for this is simple.
November 19, 1973

Fundy is within a day's ride of probably the greatest concentration of population in North America. Fundy draws visitors from all the Atlantic provinces, plus the whole eastern seaboard of the United States, which is the heaviest settled area in the United States. As a result, it has become a very popular area for American and Canadian tourists. The most recent figures available show slightly over 700,000 visitors in an area of 80 square miles, or approximately 9,000 visitors per square mile; and of course, the whole area cannot be utilized for visitors as the bulk of it is forest and woodland which is, quite properly, conserved.
This brings up the conflict that seems to exist in national parks policy, Mr. Speaker. Instead of presenting a housekeeping bill, I had hoped that the minister would present some rational parks policy to resolve the age-old conflict between the two aspects of national parks policy-the first recreation, and the second conservation. In 1970, a series of hearings took place throughout the country in every area where a national park existed. The briefs and submissions pointed up the great conflict between the conservationists and those who thought parks should be devoted to recreational purposes. I wonder what has happened to those comprehensive reports and the submissions we heard in 1970, Maybe the minister could tell us what happened to them and, specifically, what is being done for Fundy and some other parks.
Our parks are desperately overcrowded. While I realize that many people would reserve them for conservation purposes, I think we must also realize that people are entitled to have a place for recreation, whether it be camping, picnicking, swimming or whatever is their pleasure. Surely we can strike a balance somewhere along the line and reserve one park for the nature lover and set up another for recreation purposes.
Over the years we have advocated that Fundy national park be enlarged to become an integral part of the much discussed Fundy trail.
The minister has often heard the hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster (Mr. Bell) and myself extol the beauties of the Fundy trail in this House. This trail would run from the Maine border through the southern part of New Brunswick up to St. Martin's and would co-ordinate the whole area. I know there has not been any agreement between the federal government and the province on the allocation of funds for such a project, but I have suggested in this House before that perhaps the most economic way to do it would be to extend the boundaries of Fundy national park 15 miles westward in a narrow corridor to the existing settlement of St. Martin's. This would provide the missing link between St. Martin's and the present borders of the park and would complete the Fundy trail. I do not know how many acres are involved, but the coast road along that part of the Bay of Fundy could be completed if this were done. I am sure under the terms of Clause 2 the federal government could work something out. Perhaps the provincial government would make the lands available to the federal government and they could become Crown lands. I should like to draw this matter to the attention of the minister because the time is long past when we should
National Parks Act
take action to provide adequately for the people coming to Fundy national park.
It has been estimated that by 1975, 3'/2 million visitors will be coming to New Brunswick every year and that this figure will increase by 25 per cent each year thereafter. If this is true, and if the same ratio exists as at present, in the next five years we will be getting over one million visitors. Unless something is done to extend the facilities, those visitors might as well stay home.
In his remarks the parliamentary secretary made reference to transit facilities within the park. But it is also very important to provide easy access. As the minister is probably aware, the main road to the park is very dilapidated and many tourists, especially those hauling small trailers, hesitate to use it. I think this is a proper subject for dicussion with the province. Perhaps a plan could be worked out whereby the highways to and from the park could be brought up to modern standards so that tourists from the United States and other areas would be glad to come to the park and enjoy its beauty.
I do not want to take up very much time, Mr. Speaker, because I agree with this bill. I have no quarrel with any of its provisions except that I hope that when we get to committee the minister will feel inclined to strengthen the bill to provide for the future expansion of parks. I hope he will accept some of the suggestions and criticisms made in committee. If he cannot do it with this bill, I hope that in the future he will bring in a more comprehensive plan to allocate parks for purposes of recreation and conservation. With this hope, I encourage the House to get this bill into committee so that the minister can give us his ideas.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT DELINEATING GOVERNMENT'S POWER IN DISPOSING OF PUBLIC LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few moments in which I will speak-because I wish to see this bill go before the committee-I wish to underscore the importance of consultation between the federal government and the provinces on the development of a national parks policy, particularly as, abhorrent though this may be to some, more and more people are being packed on fewer and fewer acres in our cities. This will create great pressures in the cities of Canada. We shall need the co-operation of federal and provincial as well as of other levels of government if we are to develop an adequate parks system which will satisfy the thousands upon thousands of people who must live in our urban communities.
For a few minutes I want to talk about an area that is of great importance from the standpoint of conservation and the development of a parks system. I want to speak about the Rideau River system which must be developed as a result of federal and provincial co-operation. That system extends from the national capital across the countries of Grenville, Carleton, Leeds and Frontenac down to the St. Lawrence River. The St. Lawrence has been neglected both by the federal and by the provincial government which has jurisdiction there. There is a crying need for action to be taken with respect to the river, as suggested in the CORTS study which has been lying relatively dormant for a number of years. The area ought to be redeveloped, as it has all the earmarks not only of a national park but of an area of tremendous historical significance. I ask the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, to consider reactivating that CORTS study so that within a reasonable time we can bring to fruition the plan suggested in that study. We must not overlook the historical importance of the river.
We must make a beginning by cleaning up the Rideau River. The city of Ottawa, with the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton, has embarked upon a clean-up project which affects the Rideau River in the national capital area. I suggest that is merely the tip of the iceberg of the problem. Its solution will require all the resources of the city of Ottawa, of the regional municipality and, as well, of the provincial government. In order to administer a program for reclaiming or developing historical sites and developing national parks sites and camp sites for the accommodation of people, it may be necessary for governments to establish an authority composed of representatives of the federal, provincial and perhaps affected municipal governments. I think it is important for the work with respect to that great historic river to begin. As we are talking about national parks, I want once again to urge the reclamation and development of that great river which has such tremendous potential.
I also wish to commend the minister. In the southern part of my riding the St. Lawrence divides my riding from the thirtieth congressional district of the United States. On the banks of the river at Prescott, Ontario, there is a fort under the jurisdiction of the minister-Fort Wellington. If ever there is to be found an instance of co-operation between those responsible for federal institutions and

those who influence the lifestream and lifestyle of any particular area, it is to be found with respect to Fort Wellington. I thank the minister for the co-operation he has shown me and the people of Prescott with respect to the use of the fort.
In this connection I must mention another part of the area coming under the federal government, Windmill Point, which is of great historical significance. I thank the minister not only for co-operating with Prescott and with other municipalities in the area, but for co-operating with me as the member representing the area. What has developed will, I hope, enhance the facilities for tourists in the area. As a result of this co-operation, which I am sure will be ongoing, I hope there will be an augmentation of the very worth-while programs which are undertaken by the local people in co-operation with officials of the minister's department. I want to pay particular tribute to the curator of the fort and those who work with him.
Along the St. Lawrence there are miles and miles of history. At Windmill Point, for instance, Schulz was captured in a Fenian raid and was defended by Sir John A. Macdonald, then a young lawyer in Kingston. Relationships between Canada and the United States had deteriorated to war, and that part of Ontario is of historical significance because an invasion was launched from that area into the United States.
It is important for there to be co-operation between provincial, municipal and federal governments in the development of a parks system so that the miles of history along the river, stretching perhaps from Kingston down as far as Upper Canada Village in my constituency, can be developed. As we grow older as a nation it will be important for us to look back and preserve the elements of our history which were made during our growth. Although co-operation between different levels of government is important in many areas, it is particularly important in the development of national parks, especially in the area to which I have alluded. That area will become more important as we grow more conscious of our history. It is important, as well, because it will afford a means of enjoyment for those who are congested in our cities.
I urge the minister to consider the matters I have raised. I commend him for the assistance he has given me and my constituents. I will sit down now because I do not want to delay the bill getting to committee. I felt that I had to make some brief remarks on this subject.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will speak for a few minutes only. I support this bill in principle. I believe my party does as well. I have travelled around this country a great deal and heard people here, especially Americans, say how wonderful our national parks are. In many respects they are the envy of the world. Nevertheless, I want to point to a few problems connected with our national parks system.
The fact that this bill provides for new parks is good; the suggested name changes are fine. I understand that some traffic laws are to be changed. Perhaps these are required, too. There has been concern for some years regarding traffic control in our national parks. Recently, and I do not know how widespread this practice is in our national
November 19, 1973

parks, I received representations from several senior citizen groups who had toured our national parks by bus.
I understand that on one tour each senior citizen was charged $1 for a traffic licence to get into the park. I was told this was an administrative error and should not have happened, yet the bus driver collected $1 from each senior citizen. I understand the traffic licence is for a vehicle, not for the individuals inside it.
My constituency adjoins a park that was established in the 1920s by the late Mackenzie King, Prime Minister of Canada. He represented the constituency of Prince Albert for some time. He also had the distinction of being defeated by a CCF member in 1945. This is a large wilderness park, with one townsite, called Waskesiu. A number of problems have developed over the years in northern Saskatchewan with regard to this park. Many years ago it was decided that Prince Albert national park would be a people's park, catering to the rich and poor alike. Over the years, the park policy was to allow shack tents along a certain part of Lake Waskesiu. Some years ago a number of bureaucrats decided to get rid of the shack tents and people were told they must move them. Even though the shack tents had been there for almost a generation, these people were told they would no longer be allowed. As far as I and the people of my constituency are concerned, this matter should be straightened out.
Many of my constituents had shack tents in Prince Albert national park. They were arbitrarily told they would have to move them. After some appeals, delegations to members of parliament and appeals by chambers of commerce to government, and so on, it was finally decided to slowly phase out the shack tents. There are thousands of miles of shoreline in Prince Albert national park. There are huge lakes such as Lake Waskesiu, Crean Lake and Kingsmere Lake. There are many areas of shoreline property that could be developed. I cannot understand why these shack tents were not left alone.
There is another matter that concerns the people in my area. I understand that some steps have been taken in this regard. I am referring to the lease fees which people have to pay for their cabins. At Prospect Point there are huge, palatial summer cottages. For years people paid a yearly lease of $50 or $60 for them. However, the yearly lease on small skid cabins with two or three rooms is $80 or $90. I cannot see the justice in that. I understand there have been some changes in this regard, but they are not substantial enough.
Another problem plaguing this area is the question of roads. There is one main road into the southeastern end of the park. This goes through the city of Prince Albert and carries much of the traffic from the west, North Batt-leford, Edmonton, Calgary and the western United States, which has to travel an extra 50 or 60 miles in order to get to the park. There is a road coming from the southwest and a provincial highway which is paved to the edge of the park. There are 15 or 20 miles of national park roads. They are curving, dusty and treacherous. They are not paved. For years people have been asking the parks branch of the federal government to build up and pave these roads. The parks branch has said no, one entrance to the park is
National Parks Act
sufficient. We feel that a second main road into the park is justified. Most national parks have several roads leading to them.
Prince Albert national park is basically a summer park, mainly June to September. Many people in my province are ski enthusiasts, but they have no place to ski. If the people in my home town have the money, they go to Banff or Jasper once every three years.

speechtext:
Someone says "Build a moutain." Half a million dollars was spent building a mountain east of Saskatoon. As far as I am concerned, that was the most useless expenditure ever made. It would have been better to build a ski resort in Prince Albert national park where there are some large hills. Prince Albert national park can and should be developed into a winter resort. For the people of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and western Ontario the only national parks with winter facilities available to them are Banff and Jasper. Parts of Prince Albert national park should be developed for winter use.
In general, the national parks policy is good. I hope the national parks branch does not capitulate to private interest for huge-scale development. They should basically be wilderness parks. I sometimes wonder whether money is apportioned evenly between the national parks of Canada. A great deal of money has been spent on certain "Cinderella" parks like Banff and Jasper. For years people in my area have been crying for improvements to Prince Albert national park. Very little has been done.
It takes a great deal of money to build roads through mountains. It would not be very difficult to build roads into Prince Albert national park, an area of hills, lakes, muskeg and woods. If $10,000 were invested in that park every now and then, it would be money well spent. The hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Knight) suggests that maybe they are waiting for Mackenzie King to come back.
I suggest another national park should be developed in Saskatchewan. I do not think there is a grasslands park anywhere in Canada. Some people may ask why we would want a grasslands park, because all you get there are gophers, prairie dogs and coyotes. Some of the shortgrass prairie is an element of our heritage that we should preserve. Perhaps that will happen in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill S-4 has many features. It has already been mentioned in this debate that many cities on the North American continent are becoming crowded and people are looking for greater access to rural areas, particularly parks.
I am glad to see this bill come before the House in its present form, but I wish it had contained provision for a project in which I took a great deal of interest along with many people in the upper Ottawa Valley. We received wholehearted co-operation from the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien), but I cannot say the same for the province of Ontario which I think has been very negligent in co-operating with the

November 19, 1973
National Parks Act
federal government in an effort to bring more national parks to the province.
I refer particularly to the project for an interprovincial national park which was being sponsored on the upper Ottawa River by the development committee of the town of Mattawa, the recreation club of Temiscamingue, Quebec, the chambers of commerce of both those towns and representatives of municipalities in those areas. We thought this would be a unique park among the national parks of Canada because it would be the first with an interprovincial flavour. It would take in a large area of the province of Quebec opposite the town of Mattawa, starting at a point about ten miles below the town of Temiscamingue. The northern boundary runs east of the Ottawa River to the town of Temiscamingue in Quebec, then along Highway 63 to the city of North Bay. The westerly side would be Highway 533 running from Highway 63 to a point just north of Mattawa, and from there over to the Ottawa River.
This takes in a region on the Ontario side of the river which is ideally suited for development as a national park. We also took into consideration the fact that Highway 17 would lead into the park from southern Ontario and the Ottawa-Montreal-Northern New York state region. Highway II would be the entrance from Toronto and other urban areas in the south as well as states bordering on the Great Lakes. Highway 17 would lead in from such northern cities as Sault Ste. Marie, Sudbury and North Bay. As well as being ideally situated, the park would be a tie between the provinces of Ontario and Quebec.
The people of the area, including the representatives of the various organizations which represented the public thinking on the matter, spent a great deal of time on this project. They even went to the expense of renting a train for a day and taking a number of people on a tour, using the old CPR line from Madawaska across the Ottawa River and up the Quebec side of the river to Temiscamingue. We were met on arrival there by the mayor and his council as well as by members of the Chamber of Commerce who were glad to see such an upsurge of interest in this proposed national park. The town's only industry had closed down and the future looked black. In Mattawa, the Weyerhaeuser plant was closing down and this was the only major industry in the town. The people of the area were naturally concerned.
We took this issue to the federal Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. I, along with others, had personal talks with the minister. We received positive answers. The minister went so far as to make a public statement in the town of Sturgeon Falls during one of his visits to northern Ontario. When asked about the possibility of an interprovincial national park to be established between Temiscamingue and Mattawa, he said he was definitely interested. Perhaps I could put on record pari of a report which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of May 23, 1972:
Mr. Chretien said last week in Sturgeon Falls he is definitely interested in setting aside the area as a park but the matter was now in the hands of the Ontario and Quebec governments. They must expropriate where necessary and cede the land to the federal government. "If they say yes tomorrow, I am ready to go ahead".

PUBLIC BUILDINGS-ALLEGED WASTE OF MONEY IN THE PURCHASE OF ART OBJECTS DISPLAYED OUTSIDE BUILDINGS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 14 I addressed a question to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Dube) with respect to the art monstrosities which have been placed in front of various government buildings around the city of Ottawa. At that time the minister replied that these specimens-that is a very good word-are chosen by a select committee composed of some of the best Canadian artists. He said it had been the policy of this and preceding governments to spend 1 per cent of the cost of a federal building on art surrounding the building.
Later, a written reply in response to further questioning on my part indicated that the earlier reply had been in error. On September 19 the minister informed us that the policy had only been in effect since January 4, 1965, so other governments were not implicated in this particular example of waste and extravagance.
To date there have been 133 of these so-called artistic statues placed around government buildings. The total expenditure has amounted to $2,167,997. A good deal has been said in letters to editors in defence of this expenditure. Someone has referred to those who dared criticize this use of public funds as uninformed, because in expressing an opinion on public art they were handicapped by personal limitations.
One of the persons serving on the selection committee, Mrs. Suzanne Rivard-LeMoyne, has said that the advisory committee on art speaks of the shine of Robert Murray's Haida, the $35,000 steel sculpture outside the external affairs building, in these terms:
November 19, 1973

The contrast of his work to the heaviness of the building, gives me a feeling of lightness," she says, "Its, airy, spatial, spiritual in a way".
Some editorials have been written on this matter and I select one from the Ottawa Journal of November 10 last entitled "Art for anarchy's sake". I do not think that this is an opinion that can be described as uninformed. It says, among other things:
Some mod (or mad) hipsters on the public works advisory committee are approving such trash; and the like of the sculpture, if that's the word, Haida outside the external affairs building, or the magnified intestinal writhings in the park adjacent to the National Arts Centre. Why? . . .
Nor are we against modern art, from Cezanne to Braque and from there to Pellan, Pollock and Riopelle; and lest we forget, sculptors Epstein and Moore. They and others of like genius refashioned the form and content of art to give us new insights. They are the glory of the last 100 years.
But if they changed the rules radically, others simply abandoned any and all rules. Dadaism, self-proclaimed as anti-art, was early in this century accepted as art. Though that school died a swift death, its denizens left spiritual grandchildren among us. Their claptrap of rusty welded metal and other scrap makes a wasteland of our art galleries and desecrates our public buildings.
Then the editorialist concluded by asking why the taxpayers should have to pay for these monstrosities. Those who defend the art say that the artists are trying to say something. In last weekend's Journal there was a series of replies from people who are trying to describe these so-called artistic creations. Perhaps I can give the House some of the reactions of a cross-section of the Canadian public. The title of the article is "Junk: By any other name, Ottawans don't like it". One person suggested that it be called "Abortion without demand". She explained:
As a graduate of the Ontario College of Art in the days of Arthur Lismer, Frank Carmichael. . . and other greats, my first comment to my husband on viewing this monstrosity was "There was a time when this sort of thing ended up in the junkyard, where it belonged",
Someone else suggested it be called The Crunch because it reminded her, in a vague way, of the energy crisis . . .
It could, of course, perhaps be a symbol to government waste and stupidity, but surely another monument to this combination would be redundant.
Yet another suggested that it be called "The Peace of God", adding wryly, "because it passeth all understanding". My reason for raising this matter tonight is to get an answer f'om the government that will make some sense. The question I asked on September 14 was:
Does the minister intend to accept the advice of the hon. member for Cochrane, who has advised the government either to get rid of them or to place a shroud over them, or is he going to wait until the Canadian people place a shroud over the government?

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: PUBLIC BUILDINGS-ALLEGED WASTE OF MONEY IN THE PURCHASE OF ART OBJECTS DISPLAYED OUTSIDE BUILDINGS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been requested to give an appropriate answer to the matter raised by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dins-dale). I should like, first of all, to say I have been told that politicians are not necessarily experts in this particular field of art. For that reason, on December 23, 1964, the federal cabinet, by document No. 565-64, accepted a recommendation by the then minister of public works for the adoption of a fine arts policy to be instigated by the
Adjournment Debate
Department of Public Works in all buildings and programs serving the general public directly.
I should like to quote the answer given by the minister on September 14, as reported at page 6596 of Hansard, to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Public Works does not claim knowledge in the world of art. These specimens are chosen by a select committee composed of some of the best Canadian artists. It has been the policy of this and preceding governments to apply 1 per cent of the cost of a federal building to art surrounding the building. The question of what is art is a very subjective one and I would not want to impose my tastes nor the tastes of the hon. member on the public.
I spoke to the minister this afternoon and I should like to quote what he told me:
Someone has already stated, I do not recall if it was Shakespeare or my predecessor, that "Beauty is in the eyes of the beholder". What might appears to be a monstrosity in the eyes of one person could look like a masterpiece in the eye of another, which is why the government has wisely decided to establish an advisory committee composed of artists and supported by the National Gallery and the Canada Council who review the selections of these artists and proposed works of art. Who are we, mere mortals, to predict what in the future will be regarded as a masterpiece?
Those are the words of the minister.
