speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REQUEST THAT PENSIONS BE TIED TO INCREASES IN COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, October 17, as recorded at page 6958 of Hansard, I put this question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand):
In view of the fact that most pensions that come under the responsibility of the federal government either are, or soon will be, escalated by the full percentage increase in the cost of living, would the minister seek to prevail upon Canadian National Railways so that CN pensions can also be escalated not just by 2 per cent a year but by the full percentage increase in the cost of living?
The minister's answer was to the effect that pensions are negotiated between the unions and the railway companies and that I ought to have known that Dr. Deutsch was also looking into these matters. In reply I pointed out that collective bargaining between the companies and the unions did not include any representatives at the table from those already retired and that someone had to speak for them. I also pointed out that Dr. Deutsch's terms of reference did not include this area, namely, the escalating of the pensions of railway employees already retired.
Mr. Speaker, I believe from what I see across the way that the answer to my question tonight will be given by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Guay), my good friend from the neighbouring constituency of St. Boniface which I am happy to say is now part of my city of Winnipeg. I know where my hon. friend stands on this issue. He is just as concerned about it as I am. In his riding, as in mine, there are a great many Canadian National employees, both active and retired. In fact, the Transcona shops are in his constituency.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I wish tonight that somehow we could turn the tables so that the parliamentary secretary could ask the questions and I could give the answers. If he

November 19, 1973
Adjournment Debate
were going to ask the questions, what would he say? He would say, "Mr. Speaker, does the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre not agree that it is time for Canadian National pensions to be escalated every year, not just by two per cent but by the full increase in the cost of living? "He would also say, "Mr. Speaker, does the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre not agree that this is a matter that does not get negotiated at the bargaining table? Does he not agree that the only persons who are in a position to speak for the retired employees are those in parliament ant that it is the job of the government to tell Canadian National to get in step?"
If the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport put those questions to me, as I think he would like to do and I know he would do it with feeling, my reply to him would be that I agree absolutely. I agree, indeed I insist, that the time has come for Canadian National pensions to escalate every year by the full percentage increase in the cost of living, as most other pensions now do. I would say to the second question, "Yes, I agree that since the unions are not in a position to do anything about increasing the pensions of retired employees, it is up to the government to tell the Canadian National to get in step on this issue."
Now, since those are the answers that I would give to the parliamentary secretary if he were to put the questions to me, I hope he will reciprocate and give me the same answers to my questions that I would give to him.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joseph-Philippe Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-REQUEST THAT PENSIONS BE TIED TO INCREASES IN COST OF LIVING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to say that my own personal answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is that I agree with him wholeheartedly because I believe that the retired employees whom he has mentioned should certainly have their pensions increased by the full percentage relative to the cost of living. I also feel, and I have said it many times, that the railway employees should have pensions in parity with those of Air Canada and the civil service. I agree with that wholeheartedly, and let the hon. member rest assured that I have been saying this since 1968, since the first day I came to the House.
Speaking on behalf of the department with regard to the hon. member's question as recorded at page 6958 of Hansard, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) said in reply to the hon. member on October 17 of this year that he is quite sympathetic with their representations. He is just as keen as anyone to see future and past pensioners get the best deal possible. But the point he made was that these are matters for negotiation in the case of former workers already on pension and under negotiation in the case of today's workers. Negotiations are conducted between the union and management.
The fact of the matter is that the board of directors of the CNR has approved an increase of 2 per cent in pension payments to former employees and to widows of former employees. The increase, which takes effect from January 1, 1973, applies to all employees or their widows who retired on or before December 31, 1972. This decision was in response to representations made by the general chairman of the Canadian National Railways pension board

and followed upon action taken during recent years to compensate pensioners for cost of living increases. In 1971, CNR increased individual payments by 2 per cent per year of retirement up to 1969, or more, and last year it increased by 4 per cent all pensions that had come into effect by the end of 1970, and by 2 per cent all pensions that had come into effect by the end of 1971.
The latest increase will affect over 32,000 pensioners presently receiving payments from the CN pension fund. It represents an increase of $11 million in the unfunded liability of the fund. This increase should not, of course, be confused with the pension rule changes requested by the general chairman and by a number of other labour groups for the adoption of a so-called 2 per cent per year of service formula as the basis for computing future pensions. That matter, as you are aware, is still the subject of collective bargaining and is particularly under discussion in current mediation proceedings with the non-operating unions.
I want to assure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that I am with him all the way with regard to the pensions of CNR workers.

speakerposition: subtopic
subtopic: FISHERIES-SPORTS FISHING IN WATERS OFF VANCOUVER ISLAND-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
FISHERIES-SPORTS FISHING IN WATERS OFF VANCOUVER ISLAND-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was beginning to believe that this was going to be an all-Manitoba night. First, may I say that I am pleased that the Minister of the Environment and Fisheries (Mr. Davis) is here tonight to participate. I know he is interested in this subject and I hope he will take the remarks I am going to make in the constructive sense in which I shall attempt to submit them.
On November 7 I asked the Minister of Fisheries what he planned to do to help restore sports fishing in the area around southern Vancouver Island. The minister acknowledged in his reply, as recorded at page 7624 of Hansard, that the cohoe runs were down but he did not appear to know why. He said discussions along the lines of moving the net fishermen were proceeding. I have a file full of letters from west coast fishermen describing the problem. I am sure the minister has a similar or larger file. The simple reason there are no cohoe for sports fishermen is that they are being decimated by the commercial fishermen. I, of course, do not want to stop the commercial fishing industry nor does anyone else, but a means must be devised whereby they can coexist. It is not impossible.
As the minister well knows, the fall-off in sports fishing began in 1957 when the net fleet was established at the western end of the Strait of Juan de Fuca in a move to get the salmon before the Americans did. This is the principal reason for the lack of cohoe in the fall season, but not the only reason. Expert opinion is that far too many cohoe are being killed by trollers fishing early in the Gulf of Georgia. The season opens in mid-April and cohoe are an illegal catch at that time. However, as the trollers are permitted to fish with hoochies and flashers, they catch up to one million cohoe by accident before the season opens on June 1.
November 19, 1973

It is difficult to determine exactly how valuable the sports fishing industry is to British Columbia. A Washington state study indicated that the Puget Sound sports fishing industry is worth $20 million per year. The McMynn study indicates that the B.C. salmon sports fishing industry is also worth $20 million per year. This study in 1964 estimated that 85,000 residents and 36,000 visitors were engaged in sports fishing and spent $19 million to catch only 1.6 per cent of the commercial catch. Clearly, the sports fishing industry pays a tremendous return for its share of the resource.
Mr. Roderick Haig-Brown, the world famous naturalist, estimates that there are now 300,000 sports fishermen attempting to catch fish from a supply that has been reduced to one-quarter of its former numbers. Surely all will agree that restoring these stocks is in the best interests of both commercial and sports fishermen. The people speaking for the west coast sports fishermen-naturalists, sportsmen, conservationists such as Alec Merriman, Haig-Brown, Rhys Davis, and A1 Playfair-are not moved to this cause by a selfish desire to preserve something for themselves. They believe, that with proper leadership and management there can be sufficient fishing for 300,000 or more sports fishermen without seriously diminishing commercial fishing.
I would like to commend the minister for the initiatives he has taken in the area of hatcheries. I request that he show the same initiative in controlling the times and locations of commercial fishing. It has been recommended that, first, the net fishing should either go back to the river mouth fishing of former years or at least be located where it will not have its 98lA per cent cut of the supply before the sports fisherman gets his chance at his l'/z per cent, and secondly that the commercial fishermen might well stay out of the gulf until June 15. This would enable the 3 pounds to 4 pounds springs to put on some weight and would also eliminate the killing of thousands and thousands of young cohoe and undersized Chinooks, fish which must be shaken off the hooks because they cannot be kept. At the very least, the commercial fishermen in the gulf should not be allowed to fish with hootchies and flashers.
Adjournment Debate
I urgently request the minister to give immediate consideration to this matter. We have had two very bad years for sports fishing and cannot expect our tourists to be eternal optimists. More important, hundreds of thousands of us who like to try our luck are being deprived of one of sport's greatest thrills, a good British Columbia salmon on the end of a line and jumping.

speakerposition: Minister of the Environment
subtopic: FISHERIES-SPORTS FISHING IN WATERS OFF VANCOUVER ISLAND-REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) for his thoughtful remarks. In the next few weeks we will be having negotiations with the United States in respect of the sharing of salmon catches on the west coast, and I am hopeful that as a result we will be able to arrange our affairs in such a way that the escapement of fish of interest to sportsmen will improve not only around Victoria but also in the Strait of Georgia and off the west coast of British Columbia.
The salmon runs on the west coast of British Columbia are about as good as they were 40 or 50 years ago, but in respect of species some years are good and some are not so good. The sockeye run off the west coast of B.C. this year was the biggest since World War I, but it was a disaster in Alaska. Similarly, while sockeye was up in British Columbia, other species were down. The species of interest to sports fishermen, the cohoe and spring salmon, were somewhat below average.
A few minutes ago I phoned an official in the department on the west coast whose opinion I respect, and he told me that this year the cohoe which are normally resident in the Strait of Georgia were outside of the strait during the summer in the period when they feed and take a lure. This happens periodically for reasons that our scientists do not fully understand.
The escapement past the nets toward Victoria was roughly 50 per cent greater than the volume taken by commercial fishermen. Some 600,000 passed Victoria but were not feeding. Half of them went to the rivers and hatcheries on the Puget Sound side, and the rest to British Columbia rivers. Escapement both to hatcheries and British Columbia rivers was excellent this year, but they were not feeding as they went past Victoria.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.25 p.m.
